think better of it.example: Ned was half-tempted to turn him away, but thought better of it.

do in.here: Varys will quietly make a lord of whoever murders the Targaryen girl.
do in.example: “Instead Varys will quietly let it be known that we’ll make a lord of whoever does in the Targaryen girl.”

to our sorrow.meaning: unfortunately for us; we learned it painfully
to our sorrow.here: They learned the hard way, to their pain.
to our sorrow.example: "We learned that to our sorrow, Ser Donnel," Catelyn said.

spoken out of turn.meaning: said something you should not have said
spoken out of turn.here: The speaker worries she said too much to Catelyn.
spoken out of turn.example: I hope I have not spoken out of turn, my lady. I meant no offense.

on the wrong side of the sheet.meaning: born to parents who were not married; a bastard
on the wrong side of the sheet.here: Mya Stone is a bastard. Her parents never wed, so any child would be baseborn.
on the wrong side of the sheet.example: If Mychel Redfort laid with this girl at all, it would be on the wrong side of the sheet.

an invitation to a broken neck.here: Climbing the mountain road at night, with no full moon, would mean death.
an invitation to a broken neck.example: A night ascent, with the moon not even full? Even Lysa should know that’s an invitation to a broken neck.

bear ill will.here: Varys claims he hates no one, not even the Targaryen girl he plots against.
bear ill will.example: Once I counseled King Aerys as loyally as I counsel King Robert now, so I bear this girl child of his no ill will.

no sooner than.here: Poole had just left when Tomard announced the visitor.
no sooner than.example: Poole had no sooner taken his leave than Tomard announced a visitor.

black goat of the flock.meaning: the odd one out; the disgrace of the family
black goat of the flock.here: Brynden Tully is the black sheep of his house, who quarreled with his brother.
black goat of the flock.example: Lord Hoster had called Brynden "the black goat of the Tully flock."

give the shivers.here: Dany feared she might one day be sent to join the dosh khaleen as a widow.
give the shivers.example: Still, it gave Dany the shivers to think that one day she might be sent to join them, whether she willed it or no.

pass for.here: Viserys had found wine, and something like courage to go with it.
pass for.example: From the lurch in his step, she could tell at once that Viserys had found his wine… and something that passed for courage.

goose bumps.meaning: small bumps on the skin from cold or fear
goose bumps.here: Fear made the hairs rise on Sansa's skin under the small man's stare.
goose bumps.example: Something about the way the small man looked at her made Sansa feel as though she had no clothes on. Goose bumps pimpled her skin.

bring to bay.meaning: to corner and stop someone from escaping

bring to bay.example: It had taken Robb himself and Grey Wind to bring him to bay.

catch her eye.meaning: to get someone's notice; to be seen
catch her eye.here: Arya noticed the fallen chest as she slipped past the wagon.
catch her eye.example: As she crossed in back of the wagon, a fallen chest caught her eye.

with his breeches down.here: The Greatjon jokes about catching Jaime unready and helpless.
with his breeches down.example: The Greatjon says that won't matter if we catch him with his breeches down, but it seems to me that a man who has fought as many battles as Tywin Lannister won't be so easily surprised.

charge with.meaning: to accuse formally of a crime

charge with.example: "Lord Eddard has been imprisoned. He is charged with treason. It is said he plotted with Robert's brothers to deny the throne to Prince Joffrey."

come down to.meaning: to be reduced to; to end with only
come down to.here: Only four riders were left in the joust at the end.
come down to.example: In the end it came down to four; the Hound and his monstrous brother Gregor, Jaime Lannister the Kingslayer, and Ser Loras Tyrell

for a certainty.here: The mountain clans will surely attack again, and they may not survive it.
for a certainty.example: “If we linger here, they will be on us again for a certainty, and we may not live through a second attack.”

give voice to.meaning: to say aloud what you think

give voice to.example: And as it happens, he is of age, Ned reflected, but he did not give voice to the thought.

go hard for.meaning: to be painful or difficult for someone

go hard for.example: “It will go hard for them if they don’t,” said Grand Maester Pycelle.

nothing if not.here: Jon is extremely stubborn about hoping Benjen is still alive.
nothing if not.example: but Jon Snow was nothing if not stubborn.

as makes no matter.here: The inn was nearly full; there was hardly room left.
as makes no matter.example: We're full up, or near as makes no matter.
forms: near enough as makes no matter

on his heels.here: Jaime Lannister is pursuing Edmure's retreating men.
on his heels.example: The last word we had was that Lord Piper was falling back to join your brother and his other bannermen at Riverrun, with Jaime Lannister on his heels.

pack off.meaning: to send away, rudely or hastily

pack off.example: If I pack you off now, like a child being sent to bed without his supper, they will remember, and laugh about it in their cups.

in witness.here: Dany swears her oath before the Mother of Mountains while the stars look down.
in witness.example: This I swear before the Mother of Mountains, as the stars look down in witness.

for want of.meaning: because of not having; for lack of
for want of.here: He owned a razor. He simply had not bothered to shave.
for want of.example: Three days growth of coarse black beard covered his jaw and cheeks, but if he did not shave it was not for want of a razor; the edge of his sword had the dangerous glimmer of steel that had been honed every day for hours, until it was too sharp to touch.

no appeal.meaning: no arguing; the decision is final
no appeal.here: Robb spoke as a lord, so Bran knew he could not argue.
no appeal.example: He was using the voice of Robb the Lord when he said it; Bran knew that meant there was no appeal.

mind your place.meaning: remember your rank; do not speak out of turn

mind your place.example: “Mind your place, dancing master,” Ser Meryn said.

know your letters.here: The queen asks little Sansa if she can read.

to horse.meaning: mount up; get on your horses
to horse.here: Catelyn orders her men to ride out at once.
to horse.example: “Ser Rodrik, Ser Willis, to horse,” she shouted.

go to ground.here: The hares hid from danger, or the rats hid to nibble the queen's cheese.
go to ground.example: Hares going to ground, he supposed… or rats off to nibble the queen’s cheese.

bleed off.meaning: to weaken slowly; to drain away

bleed off.example: to bleed off strength from Riverrun, goad the boy into scattering his swords.

make up for.example: Lord Tywin would do no such thing, of course, but Tyrion would make up for it if he won free.

bring up the rear.meaning: to come last in a line

bring up the rear.example: Maester Luwin brought up the rear, riding on a donkey.

take root.meaning: to grow roots; to settle and grow

take root.example: no matter how much soil was hauled up from the Vale, they could not get a weirwood to take root here.

break her fast.here: Sansa went down to eat breakfast in the Tower of the Hand.
break her fast.example: Sansa was even pleased to see Arya when she went down to break her fast.

pour out her heart.here: Sansa told the queen everything she felt, and Cersei listened sweetly.

in full stride.example: He glimpsed Timett son of Timett vault free as his mount died under him in full stride, saw a Moon Brother impaled on a Karstark spear, watched Conn’s horse shatter a man’s ribs with a kick.

get you with child.here: Joffrey crudely tells Sansa he will make her pregnant.
get you with child.example: “I’ll get you with child as soon as you’re able,” Joffrey said as he escorted her across the practice yard.

throw the dice.meaning: to take a big gamble; to risk everything
throw the dice.here: Robb has risked everything on his plan of war.
throw the dice.example: For good or ill, her son had thrown the dice.

tie her stomach in knots.meaning: to make someone very nervous or afraid
tie her stomach in knots.here: Seeing the gold cloaks makes Arya sick with fear.
tie her stomach in knots.example: The gold cloaks had not been paying her any special attention, but the sight of them tied her stomach in knots.

before his blood was cold.here: Cersei admits she plotted against Robert's son almost right after Robert died.
before his blood was cold.example: “I swore to defend and protect his children, yet before his blood was cold, I plotted to depose and murder his son and seize the throne for myself.

make her flesh crawl.meaning: to make someone feel deep disgust or fear
make her flesh crawl.example: The touch of his hand would have thrilled her once; now it made her flesh crawl.

make off with.meaning: to run away with something or someone
make off with.here: Blackwood escapes with Edmure and the freed prisoners.
make off with.example: “Greatjon Umber fired the siege towers we were building, and Lord Blackwood found Ser Edmure Tully in chains among the other captives, and made off with them all.

taken its toll.meaning: to have caused harm, damage, or wear over time
taken its toll.here: The hard fast march south has worn the men down.
taken its toll.example: His father had set a grueling pace, and it had taken its toll.

take leave of his senses.meaning: to go mad; to lose one's reason
take leave of his senses.here: Tyrion wonders if his father has gone mad.
take leave of his senses.example: Had his lord father taken leave of his senses?

take to the air.meaning: to fly up into the sky
take to the air.here: The ravens fly up as Tyrion rides near.
take to the air.example: At Tyrion’s approach they took to the air, squawking and flapping their black wings.

thrown in with.meaning: to have joined or sided with a group
thrown in with.here: The gold cloaks have sided with the Lannisters.
thrown in with.example: The talk in Flea Bottom was that the gold cloaks had thrown in with the Lannisters, their commander raised to a lord, with lands on the Trident and a seat on the king’s council.

cut them to pieces.meaning: to chop up; to kill violently
cut them to pieces.here: Jon says he could kill the unarmored men if he had to.
cut them to pieces.example: They weren’t even wearing armor, he could cut them to pieces if he had to.

hammer your sword into a plowshare.meaning: to give up war for peace; a plowshare is a farm tool
hammer your sword into a plowshare.here: Making peace now is useless if you must make weapons again tomorrow.
hammer your sword into a plowshare.example: It is no good hammering your sword into a plowshare if you must forge it again on the morrow.
forms: hammering your sword into a plowshare

put the fear in.here: A bigger man could frighten the soldiers into obeying.
put the fear in.example: “A bigger man would be able to put the fear in them, is that what you’re saying, my lord?

after a fashion.meaning: sort of; barely; in a rough way
after a fashion.here: The wounded man can walk, but only just.
after a fashion.example: He can walk after a fashion.

for the nonce.meaning: for now; for the present time
for the nonce.here: Things are good enough for the moment.

as it please your grace.meaning: an old polite form meaning if it pleases you
as it please your grace.here: Sansa begs Joffrey politely to show mercy to her father.
as it please your grace.example: “As it please Your Grace, I ask mercy for my father, Lord Eddard Stark, who was the Hand of the King.

all for naught.here: The long march south and the dead men beside the road were all wasted.
all for naught.example: The rush south, the endless forced marches, the bodies left beside the road… all for naught.

for all the gold in casterly rock.meaning: for any amount of money; for any reward
for all the gold in casterly rock.here: Tyrion would not trade places with Jaime for any amount of gold.
for all the gold in casterly rock.example: He loved his brother, but he would not have wanted to be with him in the Whispering Wood for all the gold in Casterly Rock.

only a question of time.here: If given freedom, the prisoner will surely kill someone soon.
only a question of time.example: Give him the freedom of the castle and it’s only a question of time before he kills someone.

on the morrow.meaning: an old word for tomorrow; the next day
on the morrow.here: The queen will pay a visit the next day.
on the morrow.example: I also know that on the morrow the queen will pay you a visit.

often as not.meaning: quite often; much of the time
often as not.here: On the cold Wall, Jon will be wearing gloves most of the time.
often as not.example: On the Wall, you’ll be wearing gloves often as not.

take passage.meaning: to buy a place on a ship; to travel by ship
take passage.here: Arya has no money to pay for a boat ride.
take passage.example: She had no coin to pay a ferryman or take passage on a ship.

take in the flank.meaning: to attack the side of an army
take in the flank.here: Kevan's pikemen will hit the enemy's side and push them into the river.
take in the flank.example: Once he was fully committed, Ser Kevan’s pikes would wheel and take him in the flank, driving him into the river while I brought up the reserve.

make a poor match for.meaning: to be unable to stand against; to lose to
make a poor match for.here: Wood and stone weapons are no good against bronze.
make a poor match for.example: The wars went on until the earth ran red with blood of men and children both, but more children than men, for men were bigger and stronger, and wood and stone and obsidian make a poor match for bronze.

have the stomach for.meaning: to be brave enough for something unpleasant
have the stomach for.here: Tyrion doubts the man is brave enough for the job.
have the stomach for.example: I doubt he has the stomach for it.

have the truth of it.meaning: to be right; to understand the true situation
have the truth of it.here: Ser Rodrik is right that they need men to walk the walls.
have the truth of it.example: “Yet given time… Ser Rodrik has the truth of it, we need men to walk the walls.

give pursuit.here: The enemy will be slow to chase after them.
give pursuit.example: He will be slow to give pursuit.

sue for peace.meaning: to ask or beg for peace; sue here means plead
sue for peace.here: The losing Lannisters must now ask for peace.

castles of hope.meaning: daydreams; happy plans built in the mind
castles of hope.here: Ned, alone in his dark cell, builds hopeful plans in his mind to stay sane.
castles of hope.example: He made plans to keep himself sane, built castles of hope in the dark.

butterflies in her stomach.meaning: a nervous fluttering feeling in the belly
butterflies in her stomach.example: Butterflies fluttered nervously in Sansa’s stomach.

take her chances.meaning: to risk it; to try one's luck
take her chances.here: Arya would have to risk being caught by the City Watch.
take her chances.example: If she did not get out soon, she would have to take her chances with the gold cloaks.

take them in the rear.here: Blackfish leads men across the bridge to hit the enemy from behind.
take them in the rear.example: Our spearmen formed up a shieldwall and held against their first charge, but when the Tullys saw them engaged, they opened the gates of Riverrun and Tytos Blackwood led a sortie across the drawbridge and took them in the rear.

strike his banners.meaning: to take down one's flags; to give up or change sides
strike his banners.here: The sellsword lowers his flags and joins the enemy.
strike his banners.example: He retreated in good order when he saw that the other camps were lost, with two thousand spears and as many bowmen, but the Tyroshi sellsword who led his freeriders struck his banners and went over to the foe.

like an axe through ripe cheese.meaning: very easily, as if cutting something soft
like an axe through ripe cheese.here: Jaime cut through the man easily in battle.
like an axe through ripe cheese.example: “I am told the Kingslayer went through him like an axe through ripe cheese.

alike as peas in a pod.here: The two chestnut mares look exactly alike.
alike as peas in a pod.example: Behind them, two young lordlings rode side by side on a pair of chestnut mares alike as peas in a pod.

dead on his feet.meaning: so tired one can barely stand; here, literally dead yet upright
dead on his feet.here: The dead warrior still sits upright on his charging horse.
dead on his feet.example: The man was dead on his feet, the axehead lodged in his breast, yet Shagga rode on, cleaving a shield in two with his left-hand battle-axe while the corpse was bouncing and stumbling bonelessly along on his right.

wide as saucers.meaning: opened very wide in surprise; saucers are small plates
wide as saucers.here: Bran stares in shock, his eyes round as small plates.
wide as saucers.example: Bran’s eyes had been wide as saucers, and Jon had to remind him to keep his pony in hand.

cool as snow.meaning: calm and cold; showing no feeling
cool as snow.here: Lord Tywin asks his question coldly, without feeling.
cool as snow.example: "Who might you be?" Lord Tywin asked, cool as snow.

cool as you please.meaning: calm and relaxed, as if nothing is wrong
cool as you please.here: The man stood calmly after the killing, feeling no fear.
cool as you please.example: Slit his throat in the woods, and when they found him, he stood there cool as you please and said it was some old boar did for His Grace.

dumb as a stump.meaning: very stupid; a stump is the bottom of a cut tree
dumb as a stump.here: Mormont asks if Jon thinks he was made Lord Commander for being stupid.
dumb as a stump.example: “Do you think they chose me Lord Commander of the Night’s Watch because I’m dumb as a stump, Snow?

healthy pinch.meaning: a large, generous amount; healthy here means big
healthy pinch.here: Tyrion takes a big generous pinch of salt for his meat.
healthy pinch.example: Tyrion reached a thumb and forefinger into the salt dish, and sprinkled a healthy pinch over his meat.

all about.here: The people hurry to find out why the bells are ringing.
all about.example: Everyone was moving in the same direction, all in a hurry to see what the ringing was all about.

naked sword.meaning: a sword drawn from its sheath; unsheathed
naked sword.here: Robb sits in his father's seat holding his sword drawn and ready.
naked sword.example: He remembered Robb Stark as he had last seen him, in his father’s high seat in the Great Hall of Winterfell, a sword naked and shining in his hands.

blood money.meaning: money paid to make up for a killing
blood money.here: Ulf wants to be paid because a man was killed.
blood money.example: Bronn managed to keep Shagga from chopping off the dead man’s cock, which was fortunate, but even so Ulf is demanding blood money, which Conn and Shagga refuse to pay.

bring up.meaning: to bring forward; to lead up
bring up.here: Tywin would march his army up to attack from behind.
bring up.example: While you were mounting your siege, Tywin Lannister would bring up his host and assault you from the rear.

box in.meaning: to surround so someone cannot get away
box in.here: The riders ring the boy on horseback so he cannot escape.
box in.example: A rider cut him off and turned him, and the others boxed him in, cracking their whips in his face, running him this way and that.

lay down your heavy burden.meaning: to give up a hard duty or office; to retire
lay down your heavy burden.here: The council wants Barristan to give up his office as Lord Commander.
lay down your heavy burden.example: It is the wish of king and council that you lay down your heavy burden.

exact their toll.meaning: to demand and take payment; a toll is a fee
exact their toll.here: The Freys always demand their bridge fee from travelers.
exact their toll.example: “The Freys have held the crossing for six hundred years, and for six hundred years they have never failed to exact their toll.

freedom of the castle.meaning: permission to walk anywhere inside the castle
freedom of the castle.here: Sansa may walk the castle, but guards follow her everywhere.
freedom of the castle.example: The queen had given her freedom of the castle as a reward for being good, yet even so, she was escorted everywhere she went.

go to one knee.meaning: to kneel on one knee, showing respect or loyalty
go to one knee.here: Ser Jorah kneels to Dany and calls her queen.
go to one knee.example: “My… queen,” Ser Jorah said, going to one knee.

feel it in his bones.meaning: to feel something deeply and surely, as if in the body
feel it in his bones.here: Aemon feels in his body that the cold winds are rising.
feel it in his bones.example: I can feel it in these old bones of mine, and Maester Aemon agrees.

field an army out of his breeches.meaning: to produce soldiers from nothing, as if from one's pants
field an army out of his breeches.here: Walder Frey has so many sons he could make an army from his own family.
field an army out of his breeches.example: Her father had once said of Walder Frey that he was the only lord in the Seven Kingdoms who could field an army out of his breeches.

fill their heads with.meaning: to put foolish ideas into people's minds
fill their heads with.here: Luwin says Osha is teaching the boys nonsense.
fill their heads with.example: It is unkind to repay them for their kindness by filling the boys’ heads with folly.
forms: filling the boys' heads with folly

in my stead.meaning: in my place; instead of me
in my stead.here: Aemon's brother Aegon became king instead of him.
in my stead.example: “My father was Maekar, the First of his Name, and my brother Aegon reigned after him in my stead.

in the flower of.meaning: at the best and most beautiful time of life
in the flower of.here: Ned remembers Robert as a young, handsome warrior.
in the flower of.example: He saw the king as he had been in the flower of his youth, tall and handsome, his great antlered helm on his head, his warhammer in hand, sitting his horse like a horned god.

make his match.here: Robb promised to marry a Frey girl; arranging marriages is his right.
make his match.example: My right, to make his match.

play at war.meaning: to treat war like a game; to pretend at being a soldier
play at war.here: Mormont asks if Jon is a true brother or just a boy playing at war.
play at war.example: Are you a brother of the Night’s Watch… or only a bastard boy who wants to play at war?

pull down around his ears.meaning: to destroy something over someone's head
pull down around his ears.here: Catelyn threatens to destroy the Twins' castles over Walder Frey's head.
pull down around his ears.example: I’ll pull the Twins down around his ears if I have to, we’ll see how well he likes that!
forms: pull the Twins down around his ears

put his spurs to.meaning: to kick a horse with spurs to make it gallop
put his spurs to.here: Tyrion spurs his horse and charges forward.
put his spurs to.example: Tyrion put his spurs to his horse and added one more voice to the cacophony, and the van surged forward.

put up with.meaning: to tolerate; to endure without complaining
put up with.example: Why I put up with that pestilential bird… if there was news of Lord Eddard, don’t you think I would have sent for you?

ring your bells.meaning: to hit someone hard, making their head ring
ring your bells.here: The woman threatens to hit the man.
ring your bells.example: “Here, quit your biting, or I’ll ring your bells,” the woman in the window said to the man behind her, pushing him off with an elbow.

stand aside.meaning: to step aside; to not interfere
stand aside.here: Jorah begs Dany not to make him watch her walk into the fire.
stand aside.example: You are my queen, my sword is yours, but do not ask me to stand aside as you climb on Drogo’s pyre.

strip bare.meaning: to make completely empty; to take everything away
strip bare.here: The throne room walls are left empty and bare.
strip bare.example: The walls of the throne room had been stripped bare, the hunting tapestries that King Robert loved taken down and stacked in the corner in an untidy heap.

take flame.here: In Dany's dream, the whole world catches fire.
take flame.example: “Home,” she whispered as he entered her and filled her with his seed, but suddenly the stars were gone, and across the blue sky swept the great wings, and the world took flame.

seed of the army.meaning: the small beginning from which something grows
seed of the army.here: Tyrion's three hundred clansmen are only the start of the army he wants to build.
seed of the army.example: He surveyed his ragged band of brigands: near three hundred Stone Crows, Moon Brothers, Black Ears, and Burned Men, and those just the seed of the army he hoped to grow.

throw up.here: The Freys quickly built wooden towers on both river banks.
throw up.example: It had taken the Freys three generations to complete their bridge; when they were done they’d thrown up stout timber keeps on either bank, so no one might cross without their leave.

come to grips with.meaning: to fight with; to struggle against
come to grips with.here: Jaime would be eager to fight the Stark boy.
come to grips with.example: Your brother Jaime would be eager to come to grips with him.

have a bellyful of.meaning: to be fed up with; to have had enough of
have a bellyful of.here: The speaker is sick of the Lannisters.
have a bellyful of.example: The Others take the Lannisters too, I’ve had a bellyful of them.

hew to.meaning: to stay close to; to keep to
hew to.here: Tyrion shouts to stay close to the river.

in good order.meaning: in an organized way; not in panic
in good order.here: The sellsword pulls back calmly, not in panic.
in good order.example: He retreated in good order when he saw that the other camps were lost, with two thousand spears and as many bowmen, but the Tyroshi sellsword who led his freeriders struck his banners and went over to the foe.

in the place of.here: Tywin will take Ned Stark's office as Hand of the King.
in the place of.example: “In the place of the traitor Eddard Stark, it is the wish of His Grace that Tywin Lannister, Lord of Casterly Rock and Warden of the West, take up the office of Hand of the King, to speak with his voice, lead his armies against his enemies, and carry out his royal will.

in their dust.meaning: left behind; forgotten as others rush ahead
in their dust.here: The clansmen charge off, leaving Tyrion behind.
in their dust.example: The clansmen charged after them, leaving Tyrion in their dust.

life is not a song.meaning: real life is not a pretty story
life is not a song.here: Littlefinger tells Sansa that real life is harsh, not a tale.
life is not a song.example: “Life is not a song, sweetling,” he’d told her.

take heart.meaning: to be brave; to cheer up
take heart.here: The speaker encourages Lord Hoster to be brave.

take wing.here: A raven flies up as the riders pass.
take wing.example: Distant watchers peered down from towers of unmortared stone as the party descended through the foothills, and once Tyrion saw a raven take wing.

act the part.meaning: to play one's role; to behave as expected
act the part.here: Mormont tells Jon to live up to his place as a brother.
act the part.example: I’ll expect you to act the part, henceforth.

not be far wrong.meaning: to be almost right; probably correct
not be far wrong.here: Tyrion thinks Chella's guess about enemy numbers is probably right.
not be far wrong.example: Chella’s estimate of twenty thousand men could not be far wrong.

with impunity.here: No one can kill a Lannister without being punished.
with impunity.example: No man sheds Lannister blood with impunity.

duel with a glass sword.meaning: to fight with something useless and fragile
duel with a glass sword.here: Luwin says trusting in magic is like fighting with a useless weapon.
duel with a glass sword.example: The man who trusts in spells is dueling with a glass sword.

iron gauntlet and silk glove.meaning: a hard person and a soft, charming one; a gauntlet is an armored glove
iron gauntlet and silk glove.here: Stannis is harsh like iron, Renly charming like silk.
iron gauntlet and silk glove.example: They are quite a pair, Stannis and Renly. The iron gauntlet and the silk glove.
forms: the iron gauntlet and the silk glove

the neck.meaning: a swampy narrow strip of land between the north and the south
the neck.here: Robb marches his northern army down through this swampy isthmus.
the neck.example: And now your son marches down the Neck with a northern host at his back.

dawn age.meaning: the earliest age, before kings and kingdoms
dawn age.here: The time of the very first people in Westeros.
dawn age.example: “They were people of the Dawn Age, the very first, before kings and kingdoms,” he said.

field of fire.meaning: a famous battle where Targaryen dragons burned an enemy army
field of fire.here: The great dragon victory that Catelyn remembers.
field of fire.example: “My lady, the realm has not seen such a victory since the Field of Fire.

flea bottom.meaning: the poorest district of King's Landing
flea bottom.here: The poor slum where Arya hides among beggars and thieves.
flea bottom.example: The talk in Flea Bottom was that the gold cloaks had thrown in with the Lannisters, their commander raised to a lord, with lands on the Trident and a seat on the king’s council.

kings justice.meaning: the king's executioner; the man who beheads the king's enemies
kings justice.here: Ilyn Payne, who carries out the king's death sentences.
kings justice.example: The King’s Justice must be fearsome, the master of coin must be frugal, the Lord Commander of the Kingsguard must be valiant… and the master of whisperers must be sly and obsequious and without scruple.

sworn shield.meaning: a knight sworn to guard and protect someone with his life
sworn shield.here: Sandor Clegane, sworn to guard Prince Joffrey.
sworn shield.example: “The king and council have determined that no man in the Seven Kingdoms is more fit to guard and protect His Grace than his sworn shield, Sandor Clegane.

the crossing.meaning: the guarded bridge over the river at the Twins
the crossing.here: Walder Frey's bridge, which no army can cross without his leave.
the crossing.example: Lord Tywin’s host was still many days to the south… but Walder Frey, Lord of the Crossing, had assembled a force of near four thousand men at his castles on the Green Fork.

jaqqa rhan.meaning: Dothraki for the mercy men, who kill the dying
jaqqa rhan.here: The Dothraki riders who finish off the wounded with axes.
jaqqa rhan.example: Jaqqa rhan moved among them, the mercy men with their heavy axes, taking a harvest of heads from the dead and dying alike.

mercy men.meaning: men who kill the badly wounded as a kindness
mercy men.here: The axemen cutting off the heads of the dead and dying.
mercy men.example: Jaqqa rhan moved among them, the mercy men with their heavy axes, taking a harvest of heads from the dead and dying alike.

lamb men.meaning: the Dothraki scornful name for the peaceful Lhazareen people
lamb men.here: The shepherd folk the Dothraki despise as weak like lambs.
lamb men.example: Ser Jorah said the people of this country named themselves the Lhazareen, but the Dothraki called them haesh rakhi, the Lamb Men.

hairless men.meaning: eunuchs; men who have been cut so they cannot father children
hairless men.here: The eunuch healers who treat wounds with knife and fire.
hairless men.example: “The khal sent the hairless men away, Khaleesi,” old Cohollo assured her.

milk man.meaning: an insult for a soft, unmanly man
milk man.here: Qotho's insult to the knight, calling him soft and cowardly.
milk man.example: Qotho screamed taunts at him, calling him a craven, a milk man, a eunuch in an iron suit.

my sun and stars.meaning: a Dothraki term of love for a husband
my sun and stars.here: Dany's loving name for the wounded Drogo.

the stallion who mounts the world.meaning: the promised great Dothraki conqueror of prophecy
the stallion who mounts the world.here: Dany's unborn son, promised to unite the Dothraki and conquer.
the stallion who mounts the world.example: “No man can stand before the sun of my life,” Dany said, “the father of the stallion who mounts the world.

bed of blood.meaning: a deathbed of childbirth; dying while giving birth
bed of blood.here: Lyanna died giving birth, whispering to Ned.
bed of blood.example: Promise me, Ned, his sister had whispered from her bed of blood.

bloody bed.meaning: childbirth; the bloody work of delivering babies
bloody bed.here: Mirri knows all the secrets of delivering babies.
bloody bed.example: “I know every secret of the bloody bed, Silver Lady, nor have I ever lost a babe,” Mirri Maz Duur replied.

suckling babe.meaning: a nursing baby; a helpless infant
suckling babe.here: Aemon says he was as helpless as a baby.
suckling babe.example: I was helpless as a suckling babe, yet still it grieved me to sit forgotten as they cut down my brother's poor grandson, and his son, and even the little children...

heart trees.meaning: the white weirwood trees with faces carved in them
heart trees.here: The holy trees the Starks pray to.
heart trees.example: But the Starks worshiped the old gods, the nameless gods, and if the heart trees heard, they did not speak.

black brother.meaning: a man of the Night's Watch, who wears black
black brother.here: The Watchman who once visited Winterfell.
black brother.example: And she remembered the black brother who had come to visit her father.

crow food.meaning: corpses for crows to eat; said of men about to die
crow food.here: Bronn means Tyrion's soldiers will soon be dead bodies.
crow food.example: “Crow food,” Bronn muttered beside him, giving voice to what Tyrion had left unsaid.

feed the crows.meaning: dead bodies left to be eaten by birds
feed the crows.here: The hanged Lannister scouts left for the crows.
feed the crows.example: “Not a day’s ride from here, we found two Lannister scouts feeding the crows where the Freys had strung them up.

unbowed unbent unbroken.meaning: the proud words of House Martell: never surrendered, never bent
unbowed unbent unbroken.here: The motto of Dorne, which even Aegon could not conquer.
unbowed unbent unbroken.example: Their words are Unbowed, Unbent, Unbroken.

hear me roar.meaning: the roaring words of House Lannister
hear me roar.here: Tyrion jokes, quoting his own house's proud words.

pot shops.meaning: cheap shops in Flea Bottom selling bowls of stew
pot shops.here: The stew shops where Arya might trade for food.
pot shops.example: In the Bottom there were pot-shops along the alleys where huge tubs of stew had been simmering for years, and you could trade half your bird for a heel of yesterday’s bread and a “bowl o’ brown,” and they’d even stick the other half in the fire and crisp it up for you, so long as you plucked the feathers yourself.

salt and pepper.meaning: grey mixed with black, like salt and pepper; said of hair
salt and pepper.example: At his side stood the Lord Tytos Blackwood, a hard pike of a man with close-cropped salt-and-pepper whiskers and a hook nose.

only death can pay for life.meaning: the law of blood magic: saving a life costs a death
only death can pay for life.here: Mirri's rule: to save Drogo, something must die in his place.
only death can pay for life.example: Only death can pay for life.

the things we love destroy us every time.meaning: love makes men weak and ruins them
the things we love destroy us every time.here: Mormont warns Jon that loving someone will destroy him.
the things we love destroy us every time.example: “The things we love destroy us every time, lad.

cold winds are rising.meaning: danger is coming; the Others are stirring
cold winds are rising.here: Mormont warns Jon that the dead are moving beyond the Wall.
cold winds are rising.example: "The cold winds are rising, Snow. Beyond the Wall, the shadows lengthen.

slip through her fingers.example: She let the Imp slip through her fingers.

cut off.meaning: to block someone's path; to stop them from getting past
cut off.here: The rider blocks the fleeing boy's path and turns him back.
cut off.example: A rider cut him off and turned him, and the others boxed him in, cracking their whips in his face, running him this way and that.

without their leave.here: No one may cross the Freys' bridge without the Freys' permission.
without their leave.example: It had taken the Freys three generations to complete their bridge; when they were done they’d thrown up stout timber keeps on either bank, so no one might cross without their leave.

rise through the ranks.meaning: to be promoted step by step from a low position to a high one
rise through the ranks.here: Orys Baratheon worked his way up from common soldier to great commander.
rise through the ranks.example: Orys rose through the ranks to become one of Aegon's fiercest commanders.

harden her heart.meaning: to force oneself to feel nothing; to become cold and unfeeling
harden her heart.here: Dany forces herself to feel nothing and rides on toward the gate.
harden her heart.example: She pressed her lips together and hardened her heart and rode on toward the gate.

flat nosed.example: One of them, a thick-bodied, flat-nosed woman of forty years, blessed Dany haltingly in the Common Tongue, but from the others she got only flat black stares.
flat nosed.here: With a nose that is flat and wide. One of the freed slave women Dany saves has a flat nose.

lean to.example: They put up a lean-to against the rock.
lean to.here: A small rough shelter with a sloping roof. The men build a lean-to against the rock for the night.
lean to.meaning: a small rough shelter with a sloping roof

snot nosed.example: How many men had the snot-nosed little wretch sent through that door already?
snot nosed.here: With snot running from the nose; a rude insult for a child. Tyrion thinks of the young king as a snot-nosed little wretch.
snot nosed.meaning: with a dirty, runny nose (a rude insult)

dark wings, dark words.example: "Dark wings, dark words," Ned murmured. It was a proverb Old Nan had taught him as a boy.
dark wings, dark words.here: Ned murmurs the old saying when a raven arrives, because ravens usually carry bad news.
dark wings, dark words.meaning: a Westeros saying: when ravens (dark wings) bring messages, the news (dark words) is usually bad

keep the king's peace.example: "If you cannot keep the king's peace, Janos, perhaps the City Watch should be commanded by someone who can."
keep the king's peace.here: Renly warns Janos Slynt: if he cannot keep the king's peace, someone else should command the City Watch.
keep the king's peace.meaning: to keep law and order for the king; to stop people from fighting or making trouble

the hand's tourney.example: It's the Hand's tourney that's the cause of all the trouble, my lords," the Commander of the City Watch complained to the king's council.
the hand's tourney.here: Janos Slynt complains to the king's council that the Hand's tourney is causing trouble in the city.
the hand's tourney.meaning: the tournament (a contest of fighting and riding) held to celebrate Ned Stark becoming the Hand of the King

paragraphs.context: Ser Waymar Royce was the youngest son of an ancient
paragraphs.mainIdea: Royce is a rich young knight who joined the Night's Watch only because his family had more sons than titles, and he dresses for show rather than for real fighting.
paragraphs.simple: Ser Waymar Royce is the youngest son of a noble family, so he will never inherit anything — joining the Night's Watch was his only path to honor. The paragraph lists his expensive black clothes and armor to show he cares about looking like a knight, not about the hard life of ranging. Words like destrier (a knight's warhorse), garron (a small rough horse), and sable (an expensive fur) underline how out of place he is among the rough veteran rangers.

paragraphs.context: “It was the cold,” Gared said with iron certainty. “I
paragraphs.mainIdea: Gared explains that cold kills slowly and gently, lulling its victims to sleep — a warning that the dead wildlings may not have died the simple death Royce assumes.
paragraphs.simple: Gared, who lost his ears and toes to frostbite, describes how freezing to death really works: it does not just hurt, it tricks you. First you shiver and burn with cold, then you grow weak and drowsy, and finally you sink into a warm, peaceful sleep and never wake up. His point is that the cold is a quiet killer, and his long speech also shows the old ranger's experience against the young lordling's arrogance.

paragraphs.context: Gared’s hood shadowed his face, but Will could see the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Will realizes the old ranger Gared is so insulted by Royce that he might actually kill their commander, and only the knight's fine armor would not save him.
paragraphs.simple: Gared is furious at being mocked by the young knight, and Will fears for a moment that Gared will draw his short ugly sword and murder Royce. Will is sure Royce would lose the fight: Gared's sword is battered from real use while Royce's life is not worth 'an iron bob' (a tiny coin) if it comes to blades. The moment shows how deep the hatred between the proud old ranger and the arrogant young lordling runs — and Gared only backs down at the last second.

paragraphs.context: Ser Waymar met him bravely. “Dance with me then.” He
paragraphs.mainIdea: Facing a supernatural enemy, the mocked boy-knight Royce finally shows real courage, and Will's contempt for him turns into respect.
paragraphs.simple: All through the chapter Will and Gared have laughed at Royce as a spoiled boy playing at being a knight. But when the Other comes, Royce does not run — he throws back his cloak, takes his sword in both hands, and challenges the creature to a duel ('Dance with me then'). In Will's eyes, that one brave moment turns Royce from a boy into a true man of the Night's Watch, which makes his death hit harder.

paragraphs.context: They emerged silently from the shadows, twins to the first.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Will sees that more Others are circling Royce unseen, and must choose between warning his commander (and dying) or staying silent (and living).
paragraphs.simple: Will spots four or five more of the pale creatures creeping up behind Royce, who cannot see them. As a sworn brother, Will's duty is to shout a warning — but he knows that crying out will reveal his hiding place in the tree and the creatures will kill him too. He chooses his own life and keeps silent, hugging the tree. This is the moral failure that will haunt the chapter's end.

paragraphs.context: The man had been taken outside a small holdfast in
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran recalls the frightening bedtime stories about wildlings, giants, and the Others that shape how northern children see the world beyond the Wall.
paragraphs.simple: Old Nan is the Stark children's old nurse, and her fireside stories are Bran's main source of 'knowledge' about the wildlings: she says they are slavers, thieves, and worse, and that their women once lay with the Others in the ancient Long Night and bore half-human monsters. The paragraph shows that to a seven-year-old in the North, the people beyond the Wall are creatures of nightmare — which makes the ragged, ordinary prisoner they actually find all the more surprising.

paragraphs.context: Bran’s father sat solemnly on his horse, long brown hair
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran senses that his warm, storytelling father has put on a cold, stern mask to perform his duty as a lord carrying out an execution.
paragraphs.simple: Bran loves his father as the gentle man who tells stories by the fire, but this morning Ned Stark looks like a different person: grim, solemn, distant. The metaphor of changing faces means Ned is deliberately hiding his private self and wearing his public 'lord' face, because executing a man is a lord's duty, not a father's. It is the boy's first glimpse of what ruling costs.

paragraphs.context: His father peeled off his gloves and handed them to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned recites the formal legal formula sentencing the deserter to death, naming the king and his own titles to show the execution is lawful justice, not murder.
paragraphs.simple: This is the official death sentence, spoken in ceremonial language. Ned declares he acts 'in the name of' King Robert Baratheon — 'First of his Name' means the first king called Robert — and lists his own authority as Lord of Winterfell and Warden of the North. The long list of titles is the point: the killing is done under law, with the king's authority behind it. Ice, his greatsword of Valyrian steel, is the family blade used for the deed.

paragraphs.context: His lord father smiled. “Old Nan has been telling you
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned corrects Bran's storybook idea of wildlings: the prisoner was a Night's Watch brother who broke his sacred vow by running away, which is why he had to die.
paragraphs.simple: The ragged man in black is not a wildling at all — he is Gared from the prologue, a sworn brother of the Night's Watch who fled his post. In the North, breaking the Watch's vow of lifelong service means automatic death, because a deserter who knows he will be executed if caught has nothing left to lose and will commit any crime. Ned explains the real reason for the execution after gently mocking Bran's belief in Old Nan's monster tales.

paragraphs.context: “He does,” his father admitted. “As did the Targaryen kings
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned teaches Bran the Stark creed: a ruler who orders a death must carry it out himself, face to face, or else he forgets the weight of killing.
paragraphs.simple: Ned explains why he beheaded the man personally instead of using King Robert's professional executioner. The old Stark way says that whoever passes the death sentence must swing the blade himself, look the condemned man in the eyes, and hear his last words. A ruler who hides behind hired killers, Ned warns Bran, soon forgets what death really is — and one day Bran will be a lord dispensing justice himself.

paragraphs.context: His father knelt and groped under the beast’s head with
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned pulls a broken stag's antler from the dead direwolf's throat — a stag is the sigil of House Baratheon — and the men fall into frightened silence at the omen.
paragraphs.simple: The mother direwolf, the sigil animal of House Stark, was killed by a stag's antler lodged in her throat — and the crowned stag is the sigil of House Baratheon, the king's family. Nobody says it aloud, but everyone present reads the omen the same way: a Baratheon will be the death of the Starks. The sudden uneasy silence shows that even hard men are shaken by what looks like a prophecy of doom for Ned's house.

paragraphs.context: Bran saw his father’s face change, saw the other men
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran realizes Jon deliberately left himself out of the count of Stark children so the numbers would match the five pups — because as a bastard named Snow, Jon does not count as a Stark.
paragraphs.simple: Jon argued that the five pups were meant for the five Stark children — three sons and two daughters — and the numbers fit only because Jon silently excluded himself. Though raised alongside them, Jon is a bastard, and northern custom gives bastards the surname Snow instead of a house name. Bran, only seven, understands the quiet hurt in Jon's clever plea: Jon saved the pups for his siblings while reminding everyone, and himself, that he is not truly one of them.

paragraphs.context: The gods of Winterfell kept a different sort of wood.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Winterfell godswood is a dark, ancient, frightening forest — the opposite of the sunny garden Catelyn grew up with — reflecting the harsh old religion of the North.
paragraphs.simple: Catelyn compares two sacred woods. The one at her childhood home Riverrun was bright and pleasant, with redwoods, streams, and birdsong. Winterfell's godswood is three acres of ten-thousand-year-old wild forest: dark, silent, crowded with twisted oaks and ironwoods, smelling of rot. The description tells the reader that the northern gods are old, wild, and nameless — a very different faith from Catelyn's own.

paragraphs.context: Catelyn had been anointed with the seven oils and named
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn follows the Faith of the Seven, the southern religion with named gods and formal worship, while Ned keeps the older nameless gods of the North — a religious divide at the heart of their marriage.
paragraphs.simple: Catelyn was raised in the Faith of the Seven: one god with seven faces (like the Father, the Mother, and five others), worshipped in septs by septons with incense, crystal, and song. Ned built her a small sept at Winterfell out of love, but he himself worships the old gods of the First Men — nameless spirits of the forest, shared with the vanished children of the forest. This paragraph sets up the book's two religions, which matter for weddings, oaths, and funerals throughout the story.

paragraphs.context: At the center of the grove an ancient weirwood brooded
paragraphs.mainIdea: The heart tree is a white-barked weirwood with a carved, weeping face — the sacred center of the old religion, older than Winterfell itself.
paragraphs.simple: At the middle of the godswood stands the heart tree: a weirwood with bark white as bone and leaves red like bloodstained hands. A sad face is carved into its trunk, its eyes red with dried sap, seeming to watch whoever comes near. Legend says the children of the forest carved such faces thousands of years ago, and this tree is older than the castle — it supposedly watched Brandon the Builder lay Winterfell's first stone. Northerners pray and swear oaths before these faces.

paragraphs.context: “Yes,” Catelyn agreed. The words gave her a chill, as
paragraphs.mainIdea: Every noble house has a motto ('words'), but unlike others that boast of glory, the Stark words are a grim warning — and Catelyn finds that strangeness very northern.
paragraphs.simple: Ned says 'winter is coming' and Catelyn feels a chill, because those three words are the Stark family motto. Every great house has such 'words' — most are proud boasts about honor, loyalty, or courage. Only the Starks use a warning instead of a boast: in the North, winter can last for years and kill thousands, so their motto is a promise to stay ready. Catelyn, a southerner, reflects once more on how strange and grim northerners are.

paragraphs.context: “I am always proud of Bran,” Catelyn replied, watching the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ice is a four-hundred-year-old Valyrian steel greatsword, spell-forged in a lost civilization, and its name is even older — a relic of when Starks were kings.
paragraphs.simple: Catelyn admires the sword Ice even though she hates swords. It was made in Valyria, a great empire destroyed four hundred years ago by a mysterious disaster called the Doom, when smiths worked magic ('spells') into the steel along with hammer blows — that is why the blade still shines and holds its edge. The name Ice is older than the sword itself, inherited from the age of heroes when the Starks ruled the North as kings in their own right.

paragraphs.context: His eyes found hers, and she could see how hard
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon Arryn raised Ned and Robert as his wards, then rebelled against the Mad King to protect them — which is why his death devastates Ned.
paragraphs.simple: This packs in the backstory of Robert's rebellion. As boys, Ned Stark and Robert Baratheon were sent to live with Lord Jon Arryn at the Eyrie (a common noble custom called fostering), and the childless Arryn became like a second father to them. Years later, the cruel Mad King Aerys II Targaryen demanded their heads, and Arryn chose to raise his banners in revolt rather than hand over the boys he had sworn to protect — starting the war that put Robert on the throne. So Jon Arryn is not just a dead official to Ned; he is the man who raised him and defied a king for him.

paragraphs.context: Somewhere beyond the sunset, across the narrow sea, lay a
paragraphs.mainIdea: Viserys has turned the lost kingdom into a prayer-like obsession — 'ours by blood right, taken by treachery' — while Dany quietly cannot share the dream.
paragraphs.simple: Viserys calls Westeros simply 'our land,' repeating the words like a prayer: he believes the Targaryens own it by blood right, that it was stolen from them by treachery, and that 'the dragon remembers' — meaning their house never forgives. The repetition shows how the lost throne has become his whole identity. Dany hears the same words, but they are only words to her; she has never seen this land, so her brother's holy war is a story, not a memory.

paragraphs.context: Yet sometimes Dany would picture the way it had been,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany replays the family tragedy Viserys drilled into her: her brother Rhaegar killed by Robert, King's Landing sacked, her sister-in-law Elia and her children murdered, and her father killed by the Kingslayer.
paragraphs.simple: This is the Targaryen version of how they lost the throne, as Viserys told it a thousand times. Prince Rhaegar, Dany's eldest brother, fought Robert Baratheon — 'the Usurper' — at the river Trident and died. Then King's Landing was sacked by the 'Usurper's dogs,' the lords Lannister and Stark. Rhaegar's wife, Princess Elia of Dorne, begged for mercy while her baby son was torn from her and killed before her eyes. And their father, the Mad King, had his throat cut by Jaime Lannister — 'the Kingslayer' — while the skulls of the last dragons looked down from the throne room walls. Dany never saw any of it; it is all secondhand horror.

paragraphs.context: She remembered Ser Willem dimly, a great grey bear of
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany's only happy memory is the house with the red door in Braavos, where kind Ser Willem cared for her — until he died and the servants robbed them and threw them out.
paragraphs.simple: After fleeing Westeros, Dany's only true childhood home was a big house with a red door in Braavos, with a lemon tree outside her window. Their protector there was Ser Willem Darry, a half-blind old knight who was terrifying to the servants but gentle with Dany, calling her 'Little Princess.' When he died of sickness, the servants stole what little money remained and the children were thrown out. Dany cried when the red door closed — it is the home she dreams of, not the Iron Throne.

paragraphs.context: The old woman washed her long, silver-pale hair and gently
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany grew up expecting to marry Viserys, because Targaryens wed brother to sister to keep their 'dragon blood' pure — so being sold to a Dothraki stranger is a double betrayal.
paragraphs.simple: Targaryen custom holds that the royal bloodline must stay pure: since Aegon the Conqueror married his own sisters, Targaryens have wed brother to sister for centuries, believing their Valyrian 'kingsblood' must not mix with lesser men — 'dragons do not mate with the beasts of the field.' Dany always assumed she would marry Viserys when she came of age. Learning that he plans to sell her to Khal Drogo, a foreign barbarian, shatters both her expected future and the sacred custom itself.

paragraphs.context: Would that Ned had been able to say the same.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned remembers the young Robert — a giant warrior with a warhammer — and the contrast with the fat, worn king of today is the chapter's quiet tragedy.
paragraphs.simple: Fifteen years ago, Robert Baratheon was a magnificent warrior: six and a half feet tall, clean-shaven, muscled like a hero from a story, fighting with a huge spiked warhammer that even Ned could barely lift, wearing his house's great antlered helmet. The next paragraph shows what fifteen years of kingship did to him: the muscle turned to fat, the smell of battle turned to perfume. Ned is measuring the friend he lost against the king who arrived.

paragraphs.context: He led the way between the pillars and Robert followed
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Winterfell crypt holds generations of Stark lords as stone statues with iron swords on their laps to keep their ghosts down — a custom from when Starks were Kings in the North.
paragraphs.simple: The crypt is a long underground hall where every dead Lord of Winterfell sits as a carved stone statue on a stone throne, a great stone direwolf at his feet. By ancient custom, an iron longsword is laid across each statue's lap to keep the dead man's angry spirit in its tomb — the oldest swords have rusted away entirely, and Ned idly wonders whether those ghosts now walk free. The first of these lords ruled centuries before the Targaryen 'Dragonlords' crossed the sea, when the Starks answered to no one and called themselves Kings in the North.

paragraphs.context: Brandon had been twenty when he died, strangled by order
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned's elder brother Brandon was strangled on the Mad King's orders days before his wedding to Catelyn — while their father was forced to watch — which is why Ned married Catelyn in his place.
paragraphs.simple: Brandon Stark was Ned's older brother, the true heir to Winterfell, and he was engaged to Catelyn Tully. Days before the wedding, the Mad King Aerys Targaryen had Brandon strangled — and forced their father, Lord Rickard, to watch his son die (Rickard died too). This is the personal wound behind the rebellion: Ned inherited Winterfell, the lordship, and Brandon's bride. Every mention of Brandon explains why Ned carries both grief and a dead brother's life.

paragraphs.context: “I was with her when she died,” Ned reminded the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned recalls Lyanna's deathbed: her mysterious plea 'Promise me, Ned,' the dead black rose petals falling from her hand — a secret promise whose content the book will not yet reveal.
paragraphs.simple: Ned remembers being with his sister Lyanna when she died at sixteen, in a room smelling of blood and roses. Dying, she clutched his hand and made him swear a promise — 'Promise me, Ned' — and only when he gave his word did the fear leave her eyes; then black, dead rose petals spilled from her palm as she let go of life. Ned cannot recall what happened afterward; his friend Howland Reed had to take her hand from his. The paragraph deliberately hides what the promise was — it is the central mystery of Ned's storyline.

paragraphs.context: They had come together at the ford of the Trident
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned recalls the duel where Robert killed Prince Rhaegar at the Trident: a single hammer blow that caved in the rubies on Rhaegar's armor, while soldiers from both armies scrambled for the fallen gems.
paragraphs.simple: This is how Robert won his throne. At a river crossing of the Trident, Robert met Prince Rhaegar in single combat amid the larger battle: Robert with his warhammer and antlered helm, Rhaegar in black armor with the three-headed dragon of his house worked in rubies on his breastplate. Robert's hammer smashed the rubies and the chest beneath them, killing Rhaegar in the river. Ned notes the grim, almost comic detail that afterward, men from both armies waded into the bloody water scrambling to steal the rubies knocked loose from the dead prince's armor.

paragraphs.context: Ned dropped to one knee. The offer did not surprise
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned explains what the Hand actually does — speaks with the king's voice, commands armies, drafts laws, even sits the Iron Throne — and why the offer terrifies him.
paragraphs.simple: The Hand of the King is not an honorary title: he is the second most powerful man in the realm. He speaks with the king's voice, commands the king's armies, writes the king's laws, and even sits on the Iron Throne to give judgments when the king is absent, sick, or unwilling. Robert is offering Ned a responsibility as large as the kingdom itself — ruling in his place while he feasts. The next paragraph's single line, 'It was the last thing in the world he wanted,' lands harder once the reader understands the job's crushing weight.

paragraphs.context: The Great Hall of Winterfell was hazy with smoke and
paragraphs.mainIdea: The feast hall is hung with the banners of the three great houses present — Stark's grey direwolf, Baratheon's crowned stag, Lannister's lion — mapping the political powers gathered under one roof.
paragraphs.simple: Jon describes the Great Hall during the welcoming feast: smoky, smelling of roast meat, the singer's ballad drowned out by the roar of a hundred drunken conversations. The three banner colors tell the reader exactly who is in the room: white for the Starks' direwolf, gold for the Baratheons' crowned stag, crimson for the Lannisters' lion. In one line of heraldry, Martin seats the three families whose rivalry will drive the whole story at the same table.

paragraphs.context: He was more interested in the pair that came behind
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon studies the queen's two brothers: Jaime, the golden 'Lion' whom men praise to his face but call 'Kingslayer' behind his back, and the dwarf Tyrion — establishing the book's most important sibling pair.
paragraphs.simple: Entering behind the royal children are Queen Cersei's brothers. Ser Jaime Lannister is her twin: tall, golden, green-eyed, wearing the roaring lion of his house embroidered in gold. To his face men call him the Lion of Lannister, but behind his back they whisper 'Kingslayer' — the name he earned by murdering the Mad King he was sworn to protect. Jon thinks, 'This is what a king should look like,' which is exactly the dangerous glamour Jaime carries. The paragraph sets up the central Lannister mystery: a celebrated knight with a shameful secret.

paragraphs.context: Jon had noticed that too. A bastard had to learn
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon reads the high table like a detective: his father is tense behind his courtesies, the king is drinking himself numb, and the queen sits cold as an ice sculpture — the feast's joy is a performance.
paragraphs.simple: Jon explains his survival skill: because he is a bastard, he has learned to watch people and see the truths they hide. At the high table, his father observes every courtesy but Jon sees the tightness in him; the king toasts and laughs and eats like a starving man, but he has been drinking heavily all night; beside him Queen Cersei sits as cold as an ice sculpture — she is furious that Ned took Robert down to the crypt that afternoon instead of attending to her. Nobody is actually celebrating; everyone is acting.

paragraphs.context: He had thought on it long and hard, lying abed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon has coldly mapped out everyone's future — Robb inherits, his brothers become bannermen, his sisters marry south — and realized there is no place in that world for a bastard, which is why the Night's Watch calls to him.
paragraphs.simple: Jon lies awake reasoning about his future with brutal clarity. Robb will inherit Winterfell and command armies as Warden of the North. Bran and Rickon will hold castles as Robb's bannermen. Arya and Sansa will marry heirs of other great houses and go south as ladies of their own castles. Every sibling has a scripted life — except Jon. A bastard inherits nothing and fits nowhere. That is why the Night's Watch tempts him: it is the one brotherhood where birth does not matter, because every man there gives up his name and family.

paragraphs.context: “Let me give you some counsel, bastard,” Lannister said. “Never
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion gives Jon the book's most famous advice: own your shame openly and make it armor, so no one can ever use it as a weapon against you.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion's counsel is simple and brutal: the world will never let Jon forget he is a bastard, so Jon should never forget it either — he should say it himself, first and loudest. If he wears his bastardy like armor, no insult about it can wound him, because he has already claimed it. 'Make it your strength, then it can never be your weakness.' It is the philosophy of a dwarf who has survived a lifetime of mockery by mocking himself first — and it becomes Jon's lifelong creed.

paragraphs.context: Of all the rooms in Winterfell’s Great Keep, Catelyn’s bedchambers
paragraphs.mainIdea: Winterfell survives the deadly northern winters because it was built over hot springs whose water heats the castle walls — a small summer comfort that means life or death in winter.
paragraphs.simple: This explains how anyone can live in Winterfell at all. The castle stands over natural hot springs, and the scalding water is channeled through the walls and rooms like blood through a body, warming the stone halls and the glass gardens where food grows, and keeping the ground from freezing. Open pools steam in the courtyards day and night. In summer it is a pleasant luxury; in winter, when cold kills, it is what keeps the castle alive.

paragraphs.context: “You knew the man,” she said. “The king is a
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn warns Ned that refusing the king is deadly: kings run on pride, and the Robert he remembers is not the Robert who rules now.
paragraphs.simple: Ned insists his old friend Robert would laugh off a refusal, but Catelyn corrects him with the chapter's key political lesson: the man Ned knew is gone; a king is a different creature. Kings live on pride, and Robert has ridden all the way north to heap great honors on Ned — to refuse them would be to throw them back in the king's face, which a proud king will read as defiance and remember. Catelyn even thinks of the dead direwolf with the stag's antler in its throat as she speaks: she fears a Baratheon will destroy the Starks.

paragraphs.context: That brought a bitter twist to Ned’s mouth. “Brandon. Yes.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned confesses he feels like an impostor: everything — Catelyn, Winterfell, the Handship — was meant for his dead brother Brandon, and he is only living Brandon's life.
paragraphs.simple: When Catelyn presses him to accept, Ned breaks down. He says Brandon would have known what to do — Brandon was the bold, charming heir born to be King's Hand and father to queens. Ned never wanted any of it: not Catelyn (she was Brandon's betrothed), not Winterfell, not this honor. 'I never asked for this cup to pass to me' uses the image of a cup of wine being handed around a table — the cup of destiny was meant for Brandon, and only his brother's murder passed it to Ned. It is the most vulnerable Ned ever sounds.

paragraphs.context: “The Others take both of you,” Ned muttered darkly. He
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned surrenders with an ominous memory: the last time a Stark lord went south at a king's summons, his father never came home.
paragraphs.simple: After long resistance, Ned finally agrees to go south — and seals it with a chilling line. His father, Lord Rickard Stark, once rode south to answer a king's summons (the Mad King's), and never returned: he was murdered there. The parallel is deliberate and terrifying: Ned is walking the same road his father walked, to the same kind of danger. Maester Luwin tries to comfort him — 'a different time, a different king' — but Ned's flat 'Yes' shows he is not comforted at all.

paragraphs.context: That was the only time in all their years that
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn recalls the one time Ned terrified her: when she asked about Jon's mother, he went cold as ice and forbade her ever to ask again — proving the secret matters more than their marriage.
paragraphs.simple: Catelyn once asked Ned outright whether Jon's mother was Ashara Dayne, the beautiful lady the soldiers' gossip named. It is the only time in fifteen years Ned ever frightened her. His voice went cold as ice: 'Never ask me about Jon. He is my blood, and that is all you need to know.' Then he coldly investigated which servant had gossiped, and the whispers stopped forever. For Catelyn, this is the proof that whoever Jon's mother was, Ned loved her fiercely — and that the secret is the one thing he will never share, not even with his wife. It is why she can never forgive Jon's presence.

paragraphs.context: It wasn’t fair. Sansa had everything. Sansa was two years
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya's bitter inventory of her sister's perfections — and her own plainness — ends in a flash of dry humor about Sansa's weakness with numbers.
paragraphs.simple: Arya, nine years old, lists everything Sansa can do: sew, dance, sing, write poetry, dress well, play instruments — and on top of it all, Sansa is beautiful, with their mother's high cheekbones and auburn Tully hair, while Arya has their father's long solemn face and dull brown hair (the other girls call her 'Arya Horseface'). The one thing Arya does better is ride horses — and manage household accounts, since Sansa has no head for figures. Her closing thought is pure Arya: if Sansa marries Prince Joffrey, she hopes for his sake that he has a good steward. Even in misery, she is practical and funny.

paragraphs.context: “A shade more fun than needlework,” Arya gave back at
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya and Jon are the only Stark children with Ned's solemn northern look — and as a little girl, Arya once feared that meant she was a bastard too, until Jon reassured her.
paragraphs.simple: Of all the Stark children, only Arya and Jon look like their father: long-faced, solemn, brown-haired. Robb, Sansa, Bran, and even little Rickon all take after the Tullys, with easy smiles and reddish hair. When Arya was small, she was terrified that sharing Jon's face meant she must be a bastard like him — and it was Jon she ran to with that fear, and Jon who comforted her. The paragraph explains their special closeness: they are the two outsiders of the family, bonded by a shared face.

paragraphs.context: Arya looked. An ornate shield had been embroidered on the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Joffrey wears his arms divided between the royal stag and the Lannister lion — and Jon reads it as the Lannisters declaring themselves equal to the king.
paragraphs.simple: Arya examines the shield embroidered on Prince Joffrey's surcoat: it is split down the middle, with the crowned stag of House Baratheon on one side and the lion of House Lannister on the other. Jon's commentary cuts through the heraldry: normally the royal sigil alone would be honor enough for a prince, but Joffrey displays his mother's house as an equal partner to his father's. It is a small, arrogant statement — the Lannisters consider themselves as great as the king himself — and Jon spots it instantly.

paragraphs.context: Joffrey feigned a yawn and turned to his younger brother.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Joffrey ends the yard confrontation with icy contempt, dismissing Robb — who is actually older than him — as a child at play.
paragraphs.simple: After refusing to fight Robb with blunted tourney swords and letting his burned bodyguard Sandor Clegane bully the master-at-arms, Joffrey delivers the killing insult: he yawns, calls his little brother away, and declares 'the hour of play is done' — leave the children to their games. The cruelty is that Joffrey is twelve and Robb is fourteen; by calling the older boy a child, Joffrey uses his rank as crown prince to humiliate him in front of everyone. Robb's curses and Ser Rodrik's beet-red fury show how deeply the insult lands.

paragraphs.context: Bran was going to be a knight himself someday, one
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran dreams of joining the Kingsguard, and the legendary names he recites sketch centuries of Westerosi history — including the civil war called the Dance of the Dragons.
paragraphs.simple: Bran wants to grow up to be one of the Kingsguard: the seven greatest knights in the realm, who wear white armor, take no wives or children, and live only to guard the king. The names he lists like music are history lessons in disguise: Serwyn of the Mirror Shield and Prince Aemon the Dragonknight are ancient heroes; the twins Ser Erryk and Ser Arryk killed each other when brother fought sister in the Dance of the Dragons, a Targaryen civil war; Ser Arthur Dayne, the Sword of the Morning, is the knight Ned slew. To a seven-year-old, these are songs; to the reader, they are the deep past of this world.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t play the fool. Stannis and Renly are one thing,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Eavesdropping, Bran overhears a mysterious couple plotting: the woman fears Ned because Robert loves and listens to him, and she wishes her own man had been named Hand instead.
paragraphs.simple: Hanging outside the window, Bran realizes the unseen speakers are discussing his father. The woman is afraid: Robert loves Ned like a brother and will listen to him, which endangers 'us' — whoever they are. She says she should have insisted the king name her companion as Hand instead, but she was sure Ned would refuse. The man is lazily unconcerned: give him honorable enemies rather than ambitious ones like Littlefinger, and he will sleep easy. The reader must work out who these people are from clues — the woman's fear, the man's golden hair mentioned later — before Bran ever sees their faces.

paragraphs.context: “He betrayed one already, or have you forgotten?” the woman
paragraphs.mainIdea: The woman reveals her deepest fear: Robert still loves the dead Lyanna, and she dreads he will set her aside for a new Lyanna — exposing a rotten royal marriage.
paragraphs.simple: The woman's mask slips into raw jealousy. She calls Lyanna 'the insipid little dead sixteen-year-old' — insipid meaning dull and lifeless — and confesses she fears her husband will one day put her aside (divorce her as queen) for some new young beauty the way he still worships Lyanna's memory. She even says 'the sooner that comes to pass, the safer we'll all be' about Robert's death and her son Joffrey taking the throne. In a few lines, the reader learns the royal marriage is loveless, the queen hates her husband, and she is already imagining his death.

paragraphs.context: The queen. And now Bran recognized the man beside her.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran finally sees the lovers' faces: the queen and a man who looks exactly like her — her twin — and understands he has witnessed a deadly secret.
paragraphs.simple: Dangling from the window ledge, Bran looks up and recognizes both faces. The woman is Queen Cersei — and the golden-haired man beside her looks so much like her that they seem like mirror reflections: her twin brother, Ser Jaime Lannister. Everything clicks into place for the reader: the secret meetings, the fear of Ned, the talk of Robert's death. Bran, only seven, has stumbled onto treason — the queen in bed with her own brother — and his terrified 'He saw us' from Cersei tells the reader exactly how much danger the boy is in.

paragraphs.context: The notion seemed to delight the prince. “Send a dog
paragraphs.mainIdea: Joffrey jokes about having the Hound kill Bran's wolf — revealing his casual cruelty and his failure to grasp that the Starks would care.
paragraphs.simple: Hearing Bran's direwolf howling, Joffrey is delighted by the Hound's offer to 'silence the creature': 'Send a dog to kill a dog!' — a pun, since Sandor Clegane is nicknamed the Hound. Joffrey assumes the Starks, 'so infested with wolves,' would never miss one pup. The joke shows two things: Joffrey's instinct for cruelty disguised as wit, and his total blindness to how the Starks love these animals. Tyrion's dry reply — 'The Starks can count past six. Unlike some princes I might name' — mocks Joffrey's stupidity to his face.

paragraphs.context: “You tell your mother,” Tyrion told him. “But first you
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion slaps the crown prince twice and dictates the exact groveling apology Joffrey must deliver to the Starks — enforcing the courtesy Joffrey's rank demands but his nature lacks.
paragraphs.simple: When Joffrey sneers that the dying Bran is 'nothing to me' and refuses to offer comfort, Tyrion slaps him hard across the face — twice — and then scripts the apology word for word: Joffrey must go to Ned and Catelyn, fall to his knees, say how sorry he is, place himself at their service, and promise his prayers. Tyrion is teaching raw politics: a prince's absence at such a moment is 'noted' by everyone, and courtesy is not kindness but duty. The scene also shows Tyrion is one of the few people alive who dares strike the crown prince — and that Joffrey will remember it.

paragraphs.context: “The gods alone know,” Tyrion told her. “The maester only
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion reports something uncanny: Bran's wolf howls outside his window day and night, and when the maester closed the window, Bran's heartbeat weakened.
paragraphs.simple: Bran lies comatose with a broken back, kept alive on honey and water. But Tyrion has noticed something the maester half-admits: the direwolf pup never leaves Bran's window, howling day and night, and it always returns when chased away. Once, when they shut the window to block the noise, Bran seemed to weaken; when they opened it again, his heart beat stronger. Whether it is magic or devotion, the wolf and the boy are bound together — the first hint in the book of the supernatural link between the Stark children and their wolves.

paragraphs.context: Tyrion replied with a shrug that accentuated the twist of
paragraphs.mainIdea: When Jaime says a crippled Bran would be better off dead, Tyrion — a dwarf — answers for all 'grotesques': death is final, but life is full of possibilities.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime argues it would be a mercy to end Bran's torment: even if the boy lives, he will be 'a grotesque,' worse than a cripple. Tyrion, himself a dwarf who has heard such judgments all his life, replies with quiet steel: 'Speaking for the grotesques, I beg to differ. Death is so terribly final, while life is full of possibilities.' It is both a defense of Bran and of himself — a refusal to let the able-bodied decide that a broken life is not worth living. Jaime calls him a 'perverse little imp,' but the words linger as the chapter's moral center.

paragraphs.context: “I prayed for it,” she said dully. “He was my
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn confesses her guilt: she prayed seven times that Ned would leave Bran at Winterfell — and Bran fell from the tower, which she reads as her prayer being horribly answered.
paragraphs.simple: Speaking half to herself, Catelyn tells Jon that Bran was her 'special boy' and that she went to the sept and prayed seven times to the seven faces of god that Ned would change his mind and let Bran stay home with her. Then Bran fell. Catelyn believes her prayer was answered in the cruelest possible way: Bran is staying at Winterfell, but as a broken, dying boy who will never leave. Her flat, dull voice shows a mother drowning in guilt, and Jon's awkward 'It wasn't your fault' cannot reach her.

paragraphs.context: “It should have been you,” she told him. Then she
paragraphs.mainIdea: As Jon leaves, Catelyn calls him by his name for the first time — only to tell him she wishes he had fallen instead of Bran.
paragraphs.simple: Jon is at the door when Catelyn speaks his name — 'Jon' — for the first time ever; she has always refused to name him. He turns, hoping for some softening, and she delivers the cruelest sentence in the chapter: 'It should have been you.' She means it should have been the bastard who fell from the tower and lies broken, not her trueborn son. Then she turns back to Bran and weeps — the first time Jon has ever seen her cry. He walks the long road down to the yard carrying those five words.
