paragraphs.context: “First lesson,” Jon said. “Stick them with the pointy end.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon gives Arya a real sword — slim like the bravos use — and her first lesson is a joke that will echo through the whole series: stick them with the pointy end.
paragraphs.simple: Jon's farewell gift to Arya is a real sword, made special by the smith Mikken: slim and light like the blades the bravos (duelists) use in the Free Cities — not for hacking heads off, but for poking holes in an enemy if you are fast enough. His 'first lesson' is deliberately simple and funny: 'Stick them with the pointy end.' Arya immediately proves she knows which end that is by whapping him with the flat. The gift is a rebellion in itself: a sword for a girl, to be hidden from Septa Mordane, with a promise that Arya will find someone to teach her.

paragraphs.context: Viserys was seated just below her, splendid in a new
paragraphs.mainIdea: Viserys is humiliated because Dothraki custom seats the khal's bride above him — a 'beggar king' outranked by the sister he is selling.
paragraphs.simple: At the wedding feast, Dany sits beside Khal Drogo in the place of highest honor, while her brother Viserys sits below her — beneath the khal's bloodriders, served only after the khal and bride have refused each dish. For a man who calls himself the rightful Lord of the Seven Kingdoms, being seated lower than the thirteen-year-old sister he is trading away is an unbearable insult. He can do nothing but nurse his resentment, growing blacker with every course. The paragraph quietly inverts their power: in the Dothraki world, the bride matters and the 'king' does not.

paragraphs.context: Magister Illyrio murmured a command, and four burly slaves hurried
paragraphs.mainIdea: Illyrio's bride gift is three huge stone dragon eggs — green and bronze, cream and gold, black and scarlet — the most beautiful things Dany has ever seen.
paragraphs.simple: Inside the cedar chest, beneath the fine fabrics, Dany finds three enormous eggs, each a different color: deep green with bronze flecks, pale cream streaked with gold, and black alive with scarlet swirls. Each is so large it takes both her hands to hold, far heavier than porcelain or glass — as if made of solid stone — with tiny scales on the shell that shimmer like polished metal. Illyrio says they are dragon's eggs from the Shadow Lands beyond Asshai, turned to stone over ages yet still burning with beauty. Dany has only heard tales of such eggs; she never dreamed of holding one.

paragraphs.context: The silver horse leapt the flames as if she had
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany's triumphant ride on her wedding gift — culminating in leaping a firepit — is the first moment she feels powerful instead of afraid, and even Drogo smiles.
paragraphs.simple: Mounted on the silver filly Drogo gave her, Dany discovers she can ride: the horse answers the lightest touch, and exhilaration replaces terror for the first time in the whole book. When a firepit blocks her path with no room to stop, a daring she never knew fills her and she gives the filly her head — the silver horse leaps the flames 'as if she had wings' while the Dothraki hoot and cheer. Her message back to Drogo, 'he has given me the wind,' makes her new husband smile for the first time. It is Dany's first victory: on horseback, she is not a victim but a rider.

paragraphs.context: “Her name was Wylla,” Ned replied with cool courtesy, “and
paragraphs.mainIdea: Pressed about Jon's mother, Ned names her once — Wylla — and then shuts the subject down forever, calling it his dishonor.
paragraphs.simple: Robert teases Ned about the common girl who gave him his bastard, guessing names — Becca? Aleena? Merryl? — until Ned answers with icy politeness: 'Her name was Wylla, and I would sooner not speak of her.' When Robert presses for what she looked like, Ned's mouth tightens: 'Nor will I. Leave it be, Robert, for the love you say you bear me. I dishonored myself and I dishonored Catelyn, in the sight of gods and men.' It is the only time in the book Ned names Jon's mother — and the cold finality of 'leave it be' warns even the king not to ask again. The reader should note how little Ned actually says: one name, and a wall.

paragraphs.context: Ned did not feign surprise; Robert’s hatred of the Targaryens
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned recalls the quarrel that nearly ended his friendship with Robert: Tywin Lannister murdered Rhaegar's infant children as a 'gift,' and Robert approved.
paragraphs.simple: This is the backstory of Ned and Robert's deepest wound. When King's Landing fell, Tywin Lannister presented Robert with the corpses of Rhaegar's wife and children — a little girl dragged from under her bed, a baby boy torn from his mother's breast and dashed against a wall — as a token of loyalty. Ned called it murder; Robert called it war. When Ned protested they were only babes, the new king answered, 'I see no babes. Only dragonspawn.' Not even Jon Arryn could calm Robert's fury, and Ned rode out that day in cold rage to finish the war alone. Only Lyanna's death, and their shared grief, reconciled them. The paragraph explains why Ned both loves Robert and cannot trust his mercy.

paragraphs.context: The war had raged for close to a year. Lords
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned explains Tywin Lannister's treachery: the Lannisters sat out the whole rebellion, then arrived at King's Landing professing loyalty — and the Mad King opened his gates to them.
paragraphs.simple: Throughout the nearly year-long rebellion, the powerful Lannisters ignored calls to arms from both sides, waiting to see who would win. Then Lord Tywin appeared before King's Landing with twelve thousand men, professing loyalty to the Mad King — and Aerys, in his last mad act, ordered the city gates opened to the lions. It was a trap: the Lannisters sacked the city they had come to 'save.' Ned's point to Robert is that the Lannisters' loyalty is always timed to their advantage — 'treachery was a coin the Targaryens knew well,' Robert sneers, but Ned is really warning him about the family he married into.

paragraphs.context: “I cannot answer for the gods, Your Grace… only for
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned describes what he found in the throne room: the Mad King dead in his blood, and seventeen-year-old Jaime seated on the Iron Throne in his lion helm, his gilded sword still red.
paragraphs.simple: Ned paints the scene he rode into: Aerys Targaryen dead on the floor, drowned in his own blood, the dragon skulls staring from the walls, Lannister men everywhere — and Jaime Lannister, all of seventeen, sitting on the Iron Throne itself, wearing the white cloak of the Kingsguard over golden armor and a helm shaped like a lion's head, his golden sword across his legs still red with the king's blood. Ned rode the length of the hall in silence and simply stared up at him until Jaime laughed, stood, and said, 'Have no fear, Stark. I was only keeping it warm for our friend Robert.' Robert roars with laughter at the story; Ned never has.

paragraphs.context: There were eight in the party by then, not counting
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon meets Yoren, the Watch's recruiter, and his two new 'brothers' — ragged peasant boys saved from castration by taking the black — shattering Jon's heroic image of the Night's Watch.
paragraphs.simple: At a forest holdfast, the party is joined by Yoren, a stooped, lice-ridden black brother who recruits for the Watch, and his two charges: ragged peasant boys from the Fingers. Yoren introduces them with one cold word: 'Rapers.' Tyrion understands at once — in Westeros, a rapist's punishment is castration, so the Wall is the only alternative to the knife. 'Life on the Wall was said to be hard, but no doubt it was preferable to castration.' These are Jon's future brothers: not knights like his uncle Benjen, but criminals given a choice between mutilation and the Watch.

paragraphs.context: It was the only time that Vhaghar, Meraxes, and Balerion
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion's history book recalls the Field of Fire: the one battle where all three Targaryen dragons fought together, burning four thousand men — including a king.
paragraphs.simple: Reading about dragons, Tyrion remembers the defining battle of Aegon's conquest. When the Two Kings — Loren of the Rock (Tyrion's own ancestor) and Mern of the Reach — met Aegon with six hundred banners and a vast army, the Targaryen forces broke and ran, and for a few moments the conquest seemed over. Then Aegon and his sisters unleashed all three dragons at once — Balerion the Black Dread, Meraxes, and Vhaghar — the only time in history all three fought together. The singers called it the Field of Fire: near four thousand men burned in a day, King Mern among them, and King Loren survived only to surrender. Tyrion is 'duly grateful' — his ancestor's surrender is why House Lannister still exists.

paragraphs.context: “Fourteen, and you’re taller than I will ever be. My
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion explains why he reads so much: his twisted body can never wield a sword, so his mind is his weapon — and a mind needs books as a sword needs a whetstone.
paragraphs.simple: Asked why he reads constantly, Tyrion gives Jon an unsparing inventory of himself: short twisted legs, a special saddle to stay on a horse, arms too short to ever make a swordsman — had he been born a peasant, he might have been left to die or sold to a freak show. But his head is large, 'just large enough for my mind,' and he has an honest grasp of his strengths and weaknesses. His brother has his sword, Robert has his warhammer, and Tyrion has his mind — 'and a mind needs books as a sword needs a whetstone, if it is to keep its edge.' A whetstone sharpens a blade; books sharpen a mind. It is Tyrion's whole survival strategy in one sentence.

paragraphs.context: Tyrion laughed. “You’re too smart to believe that. The Night’s
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion demolishes Jon's romance about the Watch: it is a dumping ground for rapers, thieves, debtors, and bastards, watching for monsters that do not exist.
paragraphs.simple: When Jon insists the Night's Watch is a noble calling, Tyrion answers with deliberate cruelty: it is a 'midden heap' — a garbage pile — for the realm's misfits. He lists Jon's future brothers: sullen peasants, debtors, poachers, rapers, thieves, and bastards. Their great enemy is imaginary: grumkins and snarks, the monsters of nursery tales — 'the good part is there are no grumkins or snarks, so it's scarcely dangerous work. The bad part is you freeze your balls off, but since you're not allowed to breed anyway, I don't suppose that matters.' Every word is designed to wound, and every word is true — which is why Jon screams at him to stop.

paragraphs.context: She reached up with both hands and grabbed the blade
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn fights the assassin bare-handed: she seizes the dagger blade, lets it cut her fingers to the bone, and bites through his palm to free herself.
paragraphs.simple: When the hired killer puts his dagger to her throat, Catelyn does not freeze — she grabs the blade itself with both hands and pulls it away, though her fingers go slippery with her own blood. When he clamps his hand over her mouth and cuts off her air, she twists her head, gets his flesh between her teeth, and bites down hard, grinding until he screams and lets go. She sucks in air and screams for help. It is a mother's ferocity, fought with teeth and bleeding hands, and it buys the seconds Bran's wolf needs to arrive.

paragraphs.context: “Someone is afraid Bran might wake up,” Robb said, “afraid
paragraphs.mainIdea: Robb works out the logic himself: someone paid to kill a helpless sleeping boy because they fear what Bran might remember when he wakes.
paragraphs.simple: Catelyn tests her son the way a lord must test an heir: 'If you are to rule in the north, you must think these things through. Why would anyone want to kill a sleeping child?' Robb answers correctly: someone is afraid Bran might wake up — afraid of what he might say or do, afraid of something he knows. Catelyn is proud: her boy has reasoned like a ruler. The logic reframes everything: Bran's fall was not an accident to be mourned but a secret to be silenced, which means the fall itself was no accident either.

paragraphs.context: “We found the knife still in the villain’s grasp. It
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ser Rodrik's discovery: the killer's dagger is Valyrian steel with a dragonbone hilt — far too fine for a stable-hand assassin, so someone rich and powerful gave it to him.
paragraphs.simple: Examining the dead killer's knife, Ser Rodrik finds something shocking: the blade is Valyrian steel — the rare, spell-forged metal worth a fortune — and the hilt is carved dragonbone. 'A weapon like that has no business being in the hands of such as him. Someone gave it to him.' A nameless cutthroat could never own such a blade; it must have come from someone wealthy enough to arm an assassin with a treasure. The dagger turns a random attack into a conspiracy — and gives them something to trace, since a blade that fine 'will not have gone unnoticed.'

paragraphs.context: “My sister Lysa believes the Lannisters murdered her husband, Lord
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn lays out her full accusation: Lysa believes the Lannisters murdered Jon Arryn, Jaime skipped the hunt the day Bran fell, and Bran was thrown from the tower.
paragraphs.simple: After swearing everyone to secrecy, Catelyn connects the pieces aloud for the first time: her sister Lysa believes the Lannisters murdered her husband Jon Arryn; Jaime Lannister pointedly did not join the hunt on the day Bran fell but remained in the castle; and now someone has paid a fortune to silence the boy. Her conclusion drops into a deathly quiet room: 'I do not think Bran fell from that tower. I think he was thrown.' It is a monstrous accusation against the queen's beloved brother — which is why she insists they need proof, and why she decides she must go to King's Landing herself, in secret, to find it.

paragraphs.context: Sansa already looked her best. She had brushed out her
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa is in love not with Joffrey but with her idea of him — the prince from the songs — which is why she cannot see who he really is.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa admits she does not really know Joffrey, yet she is 'already in love with him' because he matches everything she ever dreamed a prince should be: tall, handsome, strong, with hair like gold. Her betrothal makes her feel a 'strange fluttering inside.' The paragraph is the key to Sansa's whole character: she experiences life through songs and stories, so she loves the role — the prince — rather than the person. Everything that follows in the chapter happens because she keeps forcing the real Joffrey into the shape of the song.

paragraphs.context: At first Sansa did not notice the third stranger. He
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa studies the three new arrivals: Barristan the Bold in white, the handsome young Renly Baratheon — and the silent, terrifying Ser Ilyn Payne, the king's headsman.
paragraphs.simple: Three men arrive from King's Landing. The first two kneel in gorgeous armor: an old man in white enameled scales with the white cloak of the Kingsguard, and a strikingly handsome young man in forest-green plate carrying a gold-antlered helm. But Sansa's eyes are drawn to the third, who stands apart and silent: gaunt, pockmarked, beardless, in plain worn chainmail, with a huge two-handed greatsword strapped to his back. Her terror is instinctive — Lady growls, and Sansa shakes. The reader later learns this is Ser Ilyn Payne, the King's Justice (the royal executioner), whose tongue the Mad King ripped out with hot pincers fourteen years ago — which is why he never speaks.

paragraphs.context: “It would be my pleasure, Mother,” Joffrey said very formally.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa casts Joffrey's rescue of her as a scene from a song — comparing him to legendary knights — showing how completely stories script her reality.
paragraphs.simple: After Joffrey gallantly drives off the Hound and takes her hand, Sansa's mind immediately reaches for songs: this is just like Serwyn of the Mirror Shield saving Princess Daeryssa from giants, or Prince Aemon the Dragonknight defending Queen Naerys's honor. She gazes at Joffrey 'worshipfully' and thinks 'He was so gallant.' The paragraph shows her fatal habit: she does not see a twelve-year-old boy performing courtesy — she sees a storybook hero. Her romantic lens will make her misread every warning sign for the rest of the book.

paragraphs.context: Sansa slid off her mare, but she was too slow.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The riverside confrontation explodes: Arya cracks Joffrey's skull with her stick to save Mycah, Joffrey turns his real sword on her, and Nymeria mauls his arm.
paragraphs.simple: When Joffrey presses the point of his real sword Lion's Tooth into the terrified butcher's boy's cheek until blood blooms, Arya attacks: she swings her wooden stick with both hands and cracks it across the back of the prince's head. Everything erupts at once — Mycah flees, Joffrey whirls around roaring curses, Arya's second swing is caught on his sword, she hurls a rock, and Joffrey slashes at her with live steel, backing her against a tree. Then a grey blur: Nymeria leaps and clamps her jaws around Joffrey's sword arm, knocking him down and mauling him until Arya calls her off. In seconds, a cruel game becomes a bloody disaster that will doom both wolves.

paragraphs.context: His eldest daughter stepped forward hesitantly. She was dressed in
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa lies to the king — claiming she doesn't remember — choosing her prince over her sister, and Arya never forgives her.
paragraphs.simple: Called as the only witness, Sansa looks from her sister to her prince and chooses: 'I don't know. I don't remember. Everything happened so fast, I didn't see…' It is a lie — Ned heard her true version the night Arya vanished — and everyone in the room knows it is a lie told to protect Joffrey. Arya explodes: she flies at Sansa 'like an arrow,' knocking her down and pummeling her, screaming 'Liar, liar, liar.' In trying to save her romance, Sansa betrays her blood — and the beating she takes from her little sister is the least of what it will cost her.

paragraphs.context: “We have a wolf,” Cersei Lannister said. Her voice was
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei's quiet triumph: since Nymeria is gone, she will take Sansa's innocent Lady instead — and Robert, beaten, allows it.
paragraphs.simple: When Robert shrugs off the demand for Nymeria's skin — 'that would be a fine trick, without a wolf' — Cersei answers very quietly, her green eyes shining with triumph: 'We have a wolf.' Everyone takes a moment to understand: she means Lady, Sansa's gentle pup, who was not even there. It does not matter to Cersei. A wolf must pay for her son's humiliation, any wolf will do, and Robert — who will not fight his wife over a beast — mutters 'As you will. Have Ser Ilyn see to it.' Injustice is done not with a shout but with a shrug.

paragraphs.context: Ned stood, gently disengaging himself from Sansa’s grasp. All the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned's contempt boils over: if Robert will sign Lady's death warrant to please his wife, he should at least have the courage to swing the sword himself.
paragraphs.simple: Ned has begged — 'for the love you bear me, for the love you bore my sister' — and Robert has caved to Cersei with flat, dead eyes. So Ned throws his own creed back at the king: the man who passes the sentence should swing the sword. 'Do it yourself then, Robert. At least have the courage to do it yourself.' Robert cannot meet it; he leaves without a word, 'his footsteps heavy as lead.' It is the first open crack between the two friends: Ned sees that the king he loved will order an innocent's death and walk away from it.

paragraphs.context: They were all staring at him, but it was Sansa’s
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned takes Ice and kills Lady himself — because a northern creature deserves a clean death by a lord's hand, not the headsman's axe — and denies Cersei the skin.
paragraphs.simple: When Cersei asks suspiciously why Ned would do it himself, his answer cuts her: 'She is of the north. She deserves better than a butcher' — 'butcher' meaning Ser Ilyn Payne, the royal executioner. Ned sits with Lady awhile, ruffles her fur, and does it with his own greatsword, living his creed that the one who passes the sentence swings the sword. Then he orders four men to carry her body all the way north to bury at Winterfell: 'The Lannister woman shall never have this skin.' It is a small, cold act of defiance — Cersei wanted a trophy; she gets nothing.

paragraphs.context: Bending, Ned pulled back the cloak, dreading the words he
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Hound returns with Mycah's corpse — cut nearly in half — and his only explanation is the chilling 'He ran. But not very fast.'
paragraphs.simple: Ned braces himself to tell Arya her wolf is dead, but the bloody bundle is worse: it is Mycah, the thirteen-year-old butcher's boy, 'cut almost in half from shoulder to waist by some terrible blow struck from above.' The Hound's account is four words: 'He ran.' — and when Ned says 'You rode him down,' the Hound laughs behind his helm: 'But not very fast.' A child was hunted down on horseback and butchered for the crime of playing at knights with Arya. Ned has no words left; the chapter ends on the Hound's laughter.

paragraphs.context: Bran was staring at his arms, his legs. He was
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the dream, Bran glimpses the golden face of Jaime Lannister speaking his murderous line — and the crow frantically makes him forget it.
paragraphs.simple: As Bran falls through the dream, a shining golden face swims up out of the mist and speaks: 'The things I do for love' — the last words Bran heard before Jaime pushed him from the tower. Bran screams, and the crow attacks the memory itself: 'Not that! Forget that, you do not need it now, put it aside, put it away!' pecking at him until the face is gone. The dream is protecting Bran from a truth his waking mind cannot yet survive: he knows who threw him, but the knowledge is buried. The reader, however, is meant to remember.

paragraphs.context: He saw Winterfell as the eagles see it, the tall
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran's falling dream becomes a vision: he sees all of Winterfell from above — and the weirwood's carved face stares back at him, knowingly.
paragraphs.simple: When the crow forces Bran to look down, his dream turns into true sight. He sees Winterfell spread below like a map: Maester Luwin studying the sky, Robb practicing with real steel, Hodor carrying an anvil like a bale of hay. At the heart of the godswood, the great white weirwood 'lifted its eyes from the still waters and stared back at him knowingly.' The tree sees him seeing it — the first suggestion that the old gods are not just carvings, but something aware. Bran is not merely dreaming; he is waking into a power.

paragraphs.context: He looked south, and saw the great blue-green rush of
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran's vision shows his family surrounded by prophetic shadows: the Hound, a golden armored figure, and a stone giant full of darkness.
paragraphs.simple: Looking south, Bran sees his father pleading with the king, Sansa crying herself to sleep, Arya silently guarding her secrets — and shadows looming over them all. One shadow is 'dark as ash, with the terrible face of a hound' (Sandor Clegane); another is 'armored like the sun, golden and beautiful' (Jaime Lannister); over both looms 'a giant in armor made of stone, but when he opened his visor, there was nothing inside but darkness and thick black blood.' The dream is showing Bran — and the reader — the dangers gathering around his family in King's Landing, in images he cannot yet decode.

paragraphs.context: Finally he looked north. He saw the Wall shining like
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran looks farther north than any living man — past the Wall, past the frozen wastes — into the heart of winter itself, and what he sees terrifies him.
paragraphs.simple: Bran's sight carries him north: the Wall shining like blue crystal, Jon sleeping alone in a cold bed with 'the memory of all warmth' fleeing him — and then past the Wall, past endless snow forests, frozen shores, blue-white rivers of ice, and dead plains where nothing lives. 'North and north and north he looked, to the curtain of light at the end of the world, and then beyond that curtain.' What he finds there — 'the heart of winter' — makes him cry out in fear, his tears burning on his cheeks. The book will not say what he saw; it only tells us that the true horror of the story waits in the far north.

paragraphs.context: Catelyn was past delicacy. “He was my father’s ward. We
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn recalls who Littlefinger was: a boy raised at Riverrun who loved her, challenged Brandon Stark to a duel for her hand at fifteen, and was scarred and banished for it.
paragraphs.simple: Petyr Baelish — 'Littlefinger,' named by Catelyn's brother for his small size and his family's tiny holdings on the smallest of the Fingers — grew up as her father's ward at Riverrun, like a brother to Catelyn. But his feelings were 'more than brotherly': when Catelyn's betrothal to Brandon Stark was announced, the fifteen-year-old Petyr insanely challenged the twenty-year-old Brandon for her hand. Catelyn had to beg Brandon to spare the boy's life; Brandon let him off with a scar, and her father sent Petyr away. She has not seen him since — and burned his letter unread after Brandon's death. The reader should feel the weight of this: the cleverest man in King's Landing has loved Catelyn since childhood, and been humiliated by a Stark.

paragraphs.context: And above it all, frowning down from Aegon’s high hill,
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Red Keep looms over the city — built by Aegon, completed by Maegor the Cruel, who then executed every builder so only dragon blood would know its secrets.
paragraphs.simple: Above the sprawling city frowns the Red Keep on Aegon's high hill: seven huge drum-towers, an immense barbican, halls, bridges, barracks, dungeons, and massive curtain walls, all of pale red stone. Aegon the Conqueror commanded it built; his son Maegor the Cruel saw it completed — and then had the heads of every stonemason, woodworker, and builder who had labored on it, vowing that only the blood of the dragon would ever know the fortress's secrets. Yet now the banners on its battlements are golden, not black: where the three-headed dragon once breathed fire, now prances the crowned stag of House Baratheon. The castle itself tells the story of the Targaryen fall.

paragraphs.context: Littlefinger winced. “You don’t want to call him that. He’s
paragraphs.mainIdea: Littlefinger explains Varys's power: the eunuch spymaster's 'little birds' — informants everywhere — hear everything, sometimes before it happens.
paragraphs.simple: Asked how he found Catelyn so fast, Littlefinger credits Lord Varys, the master of whisperers — 'the King's Spider.' Varys is 'very sensitive' about the nickname, Littlefinger notes dryly; it comes of being a eunuch. His power is his network of informants, whom he calls his 'little birds': nothing happens in King's Landing without Varys knowing, and often he knows it before it happens. One of his birds heard of Catelyn's secret visit — and Varys brought the news to Littlefinger first. The paragraph establishes the capital's real currency: information, and the two men who trade in it.

paragraphs.context: “Until the tourney on Prince Joffrey’s name day,” he said,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Littlefinger claims the dagger was his until he lost it betting on Jaime at Joffrey's name-day tourney — and names the winner: Tyrion Lannister.
paragraphs.simple: Handling the Valyrian steel blade with practiced ease — flipping it, throwing it across the room to quiver in the door — Littlefinger tells its story: it was his, 'until the tourney on Prince Joffrey's name day.' He had backed Ser Jaime in the jousting, as had half the court, but Loras Tyrell unhorsed Jaime; Jaime lost a hundred golden dragons, the queen lost an emerald pendant (which she got back), and Littlefinger lost his knife. When Catelyn demands who won it, the answer drops like a stone: 'The Imp. Tyrion Lannister.' In one move, the dagger points at the queen's own brother — and the reader should notice how smoothly Littlefinger produces this perfect answer.

paragraphs.context: Benjen Stark frowned. “A boy you are, and a boy
paragraphs.mainIdea: Benjen coldly refuses to take Jon ranging and reminds him that Stark blood buys nothing on the Wall — the Watch is a new family that replaces the old.
paragraphs.simple: When Jon begs to join Benjen's ranging into the haunted forest, his uncle refuses curtly: 'This is not Winterfell. On the Wall, a man gets only what he earns. You're no ranger, Jon, only a green boy with the smell of summer still on you.' And when Jon hints that his Stark blood should win him favors, Benjen cuts him down: 'We put aside our old families when we swear our vows. Your father will always have a place in my heart, but these are my brothers now' — gesturing at the hard men in black. The genial uncle of Winterfell is gone; in his place is the First Ranger, and Jon learns that at Castle Black he starts as nothing.

paragraphs.context: “No. They hate you because you act like you’re better
paragraphs.mainIdea: Donal Noye tells Jon the hard truth: the other boys don't hate him for being better — they hate his arrogance, and his victories are bullying, not skill.
paragraphs.simple: After Jon beats up four boys in the armory, the one-armed smith Donal Noye delivers the chapter's verdict: 'They hate you because you act like you're better than they are… You're no lordling. Remember that. You're a Snow, not a Stark. You're a bastard and a bully.' Jon is stunned — he was attacked four-on-one, how is he the bully? But Noye has watched him fight: against boys who never held a real sword before, Jon's trained skill is not sport but humiliation. The word 'bully' chokes Jon because, for the first time, he sees himself through their eyes.

paragraphs.context: Donal Noye leaned forward, into Jon’s face. “Now think on
paragraphs.mainIdea: Noye explains why Jon's victories are hollow: his opponents never had a master-at-arms, never owned a real sword — Jon has been beating untrained smallfolk with a lordling's training.
paragraphs.simple: Noye lays out the truth Jon never considered: the other recruits' fathers were farmers, wagonmen, poachers, smiths, miners, and galley oarsmen. What they know of fighting they learned in alleys, taverns, and brothels; 'not one in twenty was ever rich enough to own a real sword.' Jon, trained since childhood by Winterfell's master-at-arms Ser Rodrik, has been dueling peasants with a professional's education and calling it victory. 'So how do you like the taste of your victories now, Lord Snow?' The question drains the pride from Jon's wins — and plants the seed of his turnaround.

paragraphs.context: When they finally spied Castle Black, its timbered keeps and
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon's awestruck first description of the Wall: seven hundred feet of ice, with Castle Black's keeps looking like toy blocks beneath it.
paragraphs.simple: Standing outside the armory, Jon stares up at the Wall and the description finally gives its full scale: almost seven hundred feet high — three times the tallest tower at Castle Black — wide enough on top for a dozen armored knights to ride abreast, with huge catapults and wooden cranes standing sentry 'like the skeletons of great birds' and men in black as small as ants. Beneath it, Castle Black's timbered keeps look like 'a handful of toy blocks scattered on the snow.' Older than the Seven Kingdoms, the Wall makes Jon dizzy with its weight — 'if it fell, the world fell with it.' It is the largest structure ever built by man, and Jon will spend his life in its shadow.

paragraphs.context: “The Crown is more than six million gold pieces in
paragraphs.mainIdea: Littlefinger reveals the crown is six million gold pieces in debt — half owed to the Lannisters — though the Mad King left a full treasury: Robert has beggared the realm.
paragraphs.simple: When Ned balks at the cost of Robert's tournament, Littlefinger drops the true scandal: the crown owes more than six million gold pieces. The Lannisters hold the biggest share (three million), but they have also borrowed from House Tyrell, the Iron Bank of Braavos, Tyroshi trading cartels, and even the Faith. Ned is stunned — Aerys Targaryen left a treasury 'flowing with gold.' Littlefinger's shrug says it all: 'The master of coin finds the money. The king and the Hand spend it.' Robert's feasts, tournaments, and extravagance have bankrupted the kingdom, which is why the Lannisters — the crown's creditors — hold such power over the throne.

paragraphs.context: The Lord Commander took no notice of the irritating bird.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mormont confesses the Watch's collapse to Tyrion: one deserter beheaded, two rangers lost, Benjen missing, and fewer than a thousand men left to hold a hundred leagues of Wall.
paragraphs.simple: The Lord Commander unburdens himself: he sent young Ser Waymar Royce out with two of his best men — Gared deserted (and Ned sent his head back from Winterfell), Royce vanished without a word — and now Benjen Stark, sent to search for them, is missing too. Mormont is nearly seventy, exhausted, and sees no successor: 'The Night's Watch has become an army of sullen boys and tired old men.' Of all his men, perhaps twenty can read, and fewer still can think, plan, or lead. Once, Lord Commanders spent summers building the Wall higher; now it is all they can do to stay alive. Tyrion promises to carry the plea south — while privately certain the king will ignore it, his father will mock it, and Jaime will only laugh.

paragraphs.context: “Let me tell you something about wolves, child. When the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned teaches Arya the Stark creed through the direwolf: in winter, lone wolves die and only the pack survives — so she must stop hating Sansa and stand with her family.
paragraphs.simple: Explaining why he will let her keep Needle — and why her wildness must end — Ned tells Arya 'something about wolves': when the snows fall and the white winds blow, the lone wolf dies, but the pack survives. Summer is the time for squabbles; in winter, the pack must protect one another, keep each other warm, share strengths. So if she must hate, let her hate those who would truly harm them — not Septa Mordane, and not Sansa, who is her sister: 'You may be as different as the sun and the moon, but the same blood flows through both your hearts. You need her, as she needs you… and I need both of you, gods help me.' The speech turns the family sigil into a survival rule, and it will echo through every Stark storyline.

paragraphs.context: Until the dawn of his fifteenth name day, when he
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam reveals why he is on the Wall: his father gave him a choice between taking the black and being hunted down like a pig, so the younger, fiercer brother could inherit.
paragraphs.simple: On the dawn of Sam's fifteenth name day, his father Lord Randyll took him into the woods — while skinning a deer, his arms red to the elbow — and laid out the choice. Sam, the soft, book-loving eldest son, would never be allowed to inherit Horn Hill and the Valyrian steel greatsword Heartsbane; those must go to his younger brother Dickon, 'a man strong enough to wield her.' So Sam must announce that very day that he wishes to take the black and ride north before nightfall. If he refuses, there will be a 'hunting accident': his horse will stumble, he will die — or worse, his father will hunt him down 'like the pig you are.' Ripping the deer's heart out and holding it dripping in his fist, Randyll gives the terms: 'The Night's Watch — or this.' Sam tells it in a calm, dead voice, without weeping once.

paragraphs.context: “Not yet,” Ned said. “Not until I have a better
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned recalls why Stannis inspires awe: he held Storm's End for a year of siege, starving on rats and boot leather while the enemy feasted in sight of his walls.
paragraphs.simple: Wondering why Stannis fled to Dragonstone, Ned remembers what the man is made of: during the rebellion, Stannis held his brother's castle of Storm's End through a full year of siege by the Lords Tyrell and Redwyne, surviving on rats and boot leather while the besiegers banqueted in sight of his walls. It is almost impossible to imagine what could frighten a man like that — which makes his sudden withdrawal to Dragonstone deeply suspicious. The paragraph also sketches Stannis in one line: 'stern, humorless, unforgiving, grim in his sense of duty' — utterly unlike his brother Robert.

paragraphs.context: Tyrion Lannister sniggered. That was when Catelyn knew he was
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn publicly seizes Tyrion at the crossroads inn, invoking the king's name and the honor of the riverlords present to make his arrest a matter of their duty.
paragraphs.simple: Recognizing Tyrion by his snigger, Catelyn acts in a heartbeat. She first works the room: naming the sigils of the Freys, the Brackens, the Blackwoods — riverlords sworn to her father, House Tully — and reminding each of their ties to Riverrun. Then she points at Tyrion and proclaims him a would-be child-murderer who conspired under her own roof. 'In the name of King Robert and the good lords you serve, I call upon you to seize him.' It is brilliant and reckless politics: she gives the armed strangers no time to think, binding them by honor and their king's name before Tyrion can speak. A dozen swords are drawn as one — and Catelyn has started a war.

paragraphs.context: Sansa began to cry. He let go of her then,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Drunk and bitter, the Hound tells Sansa the truth about his burned face: his brother Gregor held it in burning coals over a stolen toy — and their father covered it up.
paragraphs.simple: On the dark road home from the tourney, Sandor Clegane forces Sansa to look at his ruined face and tells her how it happened. At six or seven, he stole a wooden toy knight from his five-years-older brother Gregor — already near six feet tall and muscled like an ox. Gregor said not a word: he picked Sandor up, shoved the side of his face into a brazier of burning coals, and held it there while he screamed, until three grown men dragged him off. Their father told everyone the boy's bedding had caught fire; the maester gave him ointments — 'Ointments! Gregor got his ointments too.' Four years later, the monster was anointed a knight by Prince Rhaegar himself. 'The septons preach about the seven hells. What do they know? Only a man who's been burned knows what hell is truly like.'

paragraphs.context: That the armorer’s sullen apprentice was the king’s son, Ned
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned realizes the smith's apprentice Gendry is Robert's bastard — the Baratheon look stamped on him, especially the black hair — and Jon Arryn's dying words suddenly point somewhere.
paragraphs.simple: Visiting the armorer Tobho Mott, Ned studies his sullen blue-eyed apprentice and knows at once: 'The Baratheon look was stamped on his face, in his jaw, his eyes, that black hair.' Renly is too young to have fathered a boy this age; Stannis is too cold and honor-bound. Gendry has to be Robert's. Ned lists the king's other bastards — an acknowledged boy at Storm's End, a daughter in the Vale now seventeen or eighteen — and reflects that baseborn children threaten no one under law. But the reader should feel the click: Jon Arryn was reading about lineages, whispering 'the seed is strong,' and visiting this very smith. Every one of Robert's bastards has black hair — and the question Ned has not yet asked is what color the 'trueborn' royal children's hair is.

paragraphs.context: “I didn’t go out the gates,” she blurted. “Well, I
paragraphs.mainIdea: Chasing a cat through the dungeons, Arya overhears two plotters — one fat with a forked yellow beard — discussing the dead Hand, Ned's book and bastard, and the coming war between wolf and lion.
paragraphs.simple: Arya followed a one-eared tomcat down into the castle's dungeons and overheard two men talking by torchlight among the dragon skulls. She reports it breathlessly to Ned: 'They said you had a book and a bastard and if one Hand could die, why not a second?' — meaning Jon Arryn was murdered and Ned could be next. The fat one with rings and a forked yellow beard said they must 'delay,' but the other in mail and a steel cap said he could not keep 'juggling' — 'the wolf and the lion were going to eat each other and it was a mummer's farce.' The fat one also said 'the princess was with child.' Ned realizes the fat man matches the description of Magister Illyrio of Pentos — and that his daughter has stumbled onto a conspiracy reaching across the narrow sea.

paragraphs.context: “I wish him every success.” Ned unfastened the heavy clasp
paragraphs.mainIdea: When Robert orders the murder of the pregnant Daenerys, Ned refuses to seal the order and lays down his Hand's badge — ending their friendship over the killing of a child.
paragraphs.simple: The small council votes to assassinate Daenerys Targaryen, now pregnant with Drogo's child. Ned is the lone dissenter: 'I will not be part of murder, Robert. Do as you will, but do not ask me to fix my seal to it.' When Robert commands him as his Hand to obey, Ned unfastens the ornate silver hand clasped to his cloak — his badge of office — and lays it on the table: 'I wish him every success. I thought you a better man than this, Robert. I thought we had made a nobler king.' Robert, purple with rage, banishes him: 'make certain I never look on your face again, or I'll have your head on a spike.' Behind Ned, the council coldly resumes planning the murder — discussing the Faceless Men of Braavos — as if nothing happened.

paragraphs.context: “Make him fly,” Robert said eagerly.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lysa's six-year-old son — still nursing at her breast — eagerly demands Tyrion be thrown from the Eyrie's Moon Door, and his mad mother strokes his hair and agrees.
paragraphs.simple: The Lord of the Eyrie is Robert Arryn, a sickly six-year-old who still nurses at his mother's breast — the nipple 'wet and red' as he pops it from his mouth to ask, 'Is he a bad man?' When Lysa says Tyrion is a very bad man, the boy cries eagerly, 'Make him fly.' He means the Moon Door: the Eyrie's infamous execution, throwing prisoners out to fall screaming down the mountain. Lysa strokes her son's hair and murmurs, 'Perhaps we will. Perhaps that is just what we will do.' In four lines, Martin shows the Vale's rulers: a paranoid, grieving widow and a spoiled, stunted child playing at justice with a man's life — and Catelyn realizes her sister has gone truly mad.

paragraphs.context: Littlefinger shrugged. Rivulets of moisture twisted down the back of
paragraphs.mainIdea: Littlefinger tells Ned that Cersei had Robert's bastard twins killed and their mother sold to slavers — while Ned holds Barra, another black-haired bastard baby, and the pattern becomes undeniable.
paragraphs.simple: In the brothel, Ned finds Barra — Robert's infant daughter by a young whore — and touches her 'fine, dark hair,' black silk like Robert's own. Then Littlefinger drops the darker truth: Robert once fathered twins on a serving wench at Casterly Rock, 'too much an affront to Lannister pride, that close to home' — so Cersei had the babes killed and sold the mother to a passing slaver. Ned also remembers Lyanna's warning years ago: 'Robert will never keep to one bed… Love is sweet, dearest Ned, but it cannot change a man's nature.' Every one of Robert's children has his black hair — and Ned is now holding the proof that someone is systematically erasing that evidence.

paragraphs.context: Every khal had his bloodriders. At first Dany had thought
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany learns what bloodriders truly are: not just guards but the khal's sworn brothers, who must die with him — by suicide if needed — to ride at his side in the afterlife.
paragraphs.simple: At first Dany thought of Drogo's bloodriders as a kind of Dothraki Kingsguard, but Jhiqui teaches her it goes further: they are the khal's brothers, his shadows, his fiercest friends — 'Blood of my blood,' sharing a single life. Ancient tradition demands that when the khal dies, his bloodriders die with him to ride beside him in the night lands; if he is killed by an enemy, they live only long enough to avenge him, then follow him 'joyfully into the grave.' In some khalasars they even share his wine, his tent, and his wives — though never his horses, for a man's mount is his own. The custom reveals the Dothraki view of loyalty: absolute, unto death, without question.

paragraphs.context: And now to roll the dice, he thought with another
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion turns his 'confession' into a comic ambush: he theatrically confesses to whoring, gambling, and wishing his family dead — everything except the murders he's accused of.
paragraphs.simple: Summoned before half the Vale to 'confess,' Tyrion seizes the stage. 'I am a vile little man, I confess it. My crimes and sins are beyond counting.' He then lists them with relish: he has lain with whores hundreds of times, wished his father and the queen dead, mistreated servants, gambled, cheated, and said cruel things about the nobility — drawing chuckles, then outright laughter from the court. Lysa, purple with rage, screams 'Silence!' The trick is pure Tyrion: by confessing every petty sin with total honesty, he makes the actual charges — hiring Bran's killer, murdering Jon Arryn — look absurd by contrast. 'Those crimes I cannot confess, I fear. I know nothing of any murders.' Then he demands a trial by combat, and Lysa is trapped: she cannot deny a highborn prisoner his right.

paragraphs.context: “He told me that a maester’s collar is made of
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon argues Sam's case with Maester Luwin's lesson: a maester's chain needs every metal, as a land needs every kind of person — so the Watch should use Sam's mind instead of forcing him to be a warrior.
paragraphs.simple: Pleading for Sam's life before Maester Aemon, Jon recalls asking Maester Luwin why his collar links are all different metals. Luwin laughed: a maester forges his chain with study — gold for accounts, silver for healing, iron for warcraft — and the chain also stands for the realm: 'Lords are gold and knights steel, but two links can't make a chain. You also need silver and iron and lead, tin and copper and bronze and all the rest, and those are farmers and smiths and merchants and the like. A chain needs all sorts of metals, and a land needs all sorts of people.' Jon's conclusion: the Watch needs all sorts too — rangers, stewards, builders. 'Lord Randyll couldn't make Sam a warrior, and Ser Alliser won't either. You can't hammer tin into iron, no matter how hard you beat it, but that doesn't mean tin is useless.' Sam can read, write, do sums, and handle ravens — let him serve with his mind.

paragraphs.context: “Myrish. ‘The Seasons of My Love.’ Sweet and sad, if
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion tells the story of the first girl he ever loved: he and Jaime found her fleeing two men on the road, and Tyrion protected her.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion is whistling a sad Myrish song. He says the first girl he ever loved used to sing it. When he was thirteen, he and Jaime were riding home from Lannisport and saw her running out of the road, chased by two men shouting threats. Jaime chased the men off while Tyrion stayed to protect the frightened girl.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, you’d be astonished at what a boy can make
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion reveals he married the girl in secret, and his father found out and ended the marriage.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion says he married the girl using lies, fifty pieces of silver, and a drunken septon to perform the wedding. He set her up in a cottage, and for two weeks they played at being man and wife. Then the septon sobered and told everything to Tyrion's father, Lord Tywin. That was the end of Tyrion's marriage.

paragraphs.context: But Gunthor raised a hand. “No. I would hear his
paragraphs.mainIdea: Gunthor decides to hear Tyrion out, and Tyrion promises the clansmen the one thing they want: the Vale of Arryn itself.
paragraphs.simple: Shagga wants to kill Tyrion for mocking his axe. But Gunthor stops him: he wants to hear Tyrion's words. The clans go hungry, and steel weapons are worth more to them than gold. Gunthor asks what Tyrion will give for his life: swords, lances, armor? Tyrion smiles and answers: "All that, and more. I will give you the Vale of Arryn." ## Sentence notes (candidates)

paragraphs.context: Ned could feel cold steel against his fingers as he
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned reflects on how the Iron Throne was made from a thousand blades, melted by dragon fire and hammered for fifty-nine days, and how dangerous it still is.
paragraphs.simple: Ned feels sharp blades between his fingers. The arms of the throne end in twisted sword points, like claws. Songs say it took a thousand blades to make it, heated in the fiery breath of the dragon Balerion the Black Dread. The hammering took fifty-nine days. It is a chair that could kill a man, and some say it has.

paragraphs.context: And that may be precisely what Lord Tywin wants, Ned
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned guesses Tywin's plan is to draw Riverrun's strength away and trick the young Edmure into spreading his forces too thin.
paragraphs.simple: Ned thinks this may be exactly what Tywin wants: to bleed strength from Riverrun and provoke Edmure into scattering his men. Edmure is young and more brave than wise. He will try to defend every inch of his land, and Tywin is clever enough to know that.

paragraphs.context: Ned raised his voice, so it carried to the far
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned speaks the formal words of judgment: Gregor is denounced, stripped of all rank and lands, and sentenced to death in the king's name.
paragraphs.simple: In the full formal language of the court, Ned charges Beric's men to ride west under the king's flag and bring the king's justice to the false knight Gregor Clegane and all who shared in his crimes. He denounces Gregor, declares him guilty, strips him of all rank and titles and lands, and sentences him to death.

paragraphs.context: Sansa had no choice but to explain about heroes and
paragraphs.mainIdea: Littlefinger tells Sansa that life is not a song like the stories she loves, and she may learn that to her sorrow one day.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa has to explain to Lord Baelish why she would have sent Ser Loras: her reasons are all about heroes and monsters. He smiles and touches her cheek. He says, "Life is not a song, sweetling. You may learn that one day to your sorrow." He means the real world is not like the romantic stories Sansa loves.

paragraphs.context: Father’s mouth twitched strangely. “Sansa, I’m not sending you away
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned explains he is sending them to Winterfell for their safety: his men were murdered nearby and the king does nothing but hunt.
paragraphs.simple: Ned says he is not sending them away because they fought. He wants them back in Winterfell for their own safety. Three of his men were cut down like dogs not far from where they sit, and what does Robert do? He goes hunting. Ned means the city is no longer safe for his daughters.

paragraphs.context: “Your brother?” Ned said. “Or your lover?”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei openly admits that Jaime is both her brother and her lover, as it has been since childhood, and defends it with the Targaryen custom of marrying siblings.
paragraphs.simple: Ned asks whether Jaime is her brother or her lover. Cersei answers "Both," without flinching. It has been so since they were children. She says the Targaryens married brother to sister for three hundred years to keep the bloodlines pure. She and Jaime are more than brother and sister: they are one person in two bodies. They shared a womb. When he is in her, she feels whole.

paragraphs.context: The seed is strong, Jon Arryn had cried on his
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned lays out the proof: every child of a Baratheon and a Lannister in history has been black-haired; the golden hair always gives way to the black.
paragraphs.simple: "The seed is strong," Jon Arryn cried on his deathbed. Ned has found the proof in the records. Every time a Baratheon and a Lannister had children, the children were black-haired. Ninety years ago Tya Lannister married Gowen Baratheon, and their only child was born with a full head of black hair. Another Lannister-Baratheon match produced three daughters and a son, all black-haired. No matter how far back Ned looks, the gold always yields before the coal: Lannister gold loses to Baratheon black.

paragraphs.context: The queen stood. “And what of my wrath, Lord Stark?”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei warns Ned that he should have seized power when he had the chance, and states the book's central rule: in the game of thrones, you win or you die.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei warns Ned of her own wrath. She says he should have taken the realm for himself. When he found Jaime on the Iron Throne the day King's Landing fell, all he had to do was climb those steps and sit. "Such a sad mistake." Ned says he has made many mistakes, but that was not one of them. Cersei insists: "When you play the game of thrones, you win or you die. There is no middle ground." ## Sentence notes

paragraphs.context: “As swift as the wind he rides, and behind him
paragraphs.mainIdea: The old crone prophesies that Dany's son will be the stallion who mounts the world: a conqueror whose enemies' wives will weep tears of blood.
paragraphs.simple: The ancient crone closes her eye to see the future. She proclaims that Dany's son will ride as swift as the wind, with a khalasar of countless men behind him. He will be fierce as a storm. His enemies will tremble, and their wives will weep tears of blood and tear their flesh in grief. The bells in his hair will sing his coming. The milk men in the stone tents will fear his name. "The prince is riding, and he shall be the stallion who mounts the world."

paragraphs.context: “The stallion is the khal of khals promised in ancient
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jorah explains the prophecy: the stallion who mounts the world will be the khal of all khals, uniting the Dothraki and riding to the ends of the earth.
paragraphs.simple: Dany asks what the stallion means. Jorah explains that the stallion is the khal of khals promised in ancient prophecy. He will unite the Dothraki into a single khalasar and ride to the ends of the earth. All the people of the world will be his herd. Dany says in a small voice, "I named him Rhaego."

paragraphs.context: He was no dragon, Dany thought, curiously calm. Fire cannot
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany realizes with strange calm that Viserys was never truly a dragon, because fire cannot kill a dragon.
paragraphs.simple: "He was no dragon," Dany thinks, curiously calm. "Fire cannot kill a dragon." Viserys always called himself the dragon, but he died screaming from the heat of gold. A true dragon would not have been harmed by fire. In this one line, Dany accepts that her brother was never what he claimed to be. ## Sentence notes

paragraphs.context: “Damn you, Robert,” Ned said when they were alone. His
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dying, Robert rambles guiltily: he blames himself for Daenerys, and believes the gods sent the boar to punish him.
paragraphs.simple: Alone with Ned, Robert rambles. He killed the boar, he says, driving a knife through its eye. His thoughts turn to Daenerys: "The girl. Daenerys. Only a child, you were right… the gods sent the boar… sent to punish me…" He coughs up blood. He says it was wrong to order her death. Varys, Littlefinger, even his brother were worthless; no one told him no but Ned. Only Ned.

paragraphs.context: “I wonder, Ser Barristan,” asked Varys, so quietly, “who gave
paragraphs.mainIdea: Varys quietly hints that Robert's wine may have been the real killer: his squire Lancel, a Lannister, kept him supplied with drink.
paragraphs.simple: Very quietly, Varys asks Barristan who gave the king his wine. The wine was from the king's own skin, but there was more than one skin: the squire fetched a fresh one whenever Robert needed it. Varys calls the boy dutiful, making sure the king never lacked refreshment. The squire was Lancel, Ser Kevan Lannister's son, Tywin's nephew, the queen's cousin. Varys is hinting that the wine was no accident.

paragraphs.context: “Now look at the other side of the coin. Joffrey
paragraphs.mainIdea: Littlefinger proposes making Joffrey king under Ned's regency, marrying the Stark and Lannister children to each other, and disposing of Stannis later.
paragraphs.simple: Littlefinger turns the coin over. Joffrey is only twelve, and Robert gave Ned the regency. Ned is Hand and Protector; the power is his. All he must do is reach out and take it. Make peace with the Lannisters, free the Imp, wed Joffrey to Sansa, wed Arya to Tommen and Robb to Myrcella. In four years Joffrey will look to Ned as a second father. By then they can dispose of Stannis. And if Joffrey proves troublesome, they can reveal his secret and put Renly on the throne.

paragraphs.context: “Yes, my lord,” Jon said. The gods of the sept
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon will say his vows before a heart tree, because the blood of the First Men flows in the Starks and the gods of the sept mean nothing to him.
paragraphs.simple: Jon says yes, he will say his words before a heart tree, as his uncle Benjen did. The gods of the sept have nothing to do with him. The blood of the First Men flows in the veins of the Starks. This is why the Starks keep the old gods of the forest, not the Seven of the sept.

paragraphs.context: “The old man is Lord Commander of the Night’s Watch,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam explains that serving the Lord Commander personally means Jon will learn command, just as a lord's heir learns by standing at his father's side.
paragraphs.simple: Sam reminds Jon that the old man is the Lord Commander of the Night's Watch. Jon will be with him day and night. Yes, he will pour wine and change bed linen, but he will also carry letters, attend meetings, and squire for him in battle. He will be as close to Mormont as his shadow. Sam's father used to make his heir stand beside him at court, to watch and listen and learn. Sam wagers that is why Mormont asked for Jon: he wants to groom Jon for command.

paragraphs.context: “Gods be good,” Dywen muttered. “That’s a hand.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ghost returns from the woods carrying a severed human hand in his jaws, a chilling sign of what is happening beyond the Wall.
paragraphs.simple: Ghost stalks back between the weirwoods with something black in his jaws. Jon calls him over. Sam gasps. The old forester Dywen mutters, "Gods be good. That's a hand." A severed human hand, found in the haunted forest. Something terrible is out there. ## Sentence notes

paragraphs.context: “No,” Ned answered. “He hated rest. The gods give him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned refuses empty words about Robert's rest, and hides his grief because he is the Hand and the dreaded hour has come.
paragraphs.simple: Pycelle brings word that King Robert is gone. Ned answers, "No. He hated rest. The gods give him love and laughter, and the joy of righteous battle." He feels strangely empty. He had expected the visit, yet with those words, something dies within him. He would have given all his titles for the freedom to weep, but he is Robert's Hand, and the hour he dreaded has come. He orders Pycelle to summon the council to his solar at once.

paragraphs.context: With a single sharp thrust, the nearest gold cloak drove
paragraphs.mainIdea: The City Watch betrays Ned: the gold cloaks suddenly attack and kill Tomard and the rest of Ned's men.
paragraphs.simple: In the middle of Ned's order to take the queen into custody, the nearest gold cloak drives his spear into Tomard's back. The wet red point bursts out through Tom's ribs. He is dead before his sword hits the floor. Ned's shout comes too late. Janos Slynt himself slashes open Varly's throat. Cayn fights bravely for a moment, then the Hound cuts off his sword hand and opens him from shoulder to breastbone. All of Ned's men are dying around him.

paragraphs.context: She followed him over to the wall, where he settled
paragraphs.mainIdea: Syrio begins the story of how he became first sword to the Sealord of Braavos.
paragraphs.simple: Arya follows Syrio to a bench by the wall. Syrio says he was first sword to the Sealord of Braavos. Arya asks how that came to be. Syrio says he was the finest swordsman in the city, but that is not the whole reason. Other men were stronger, faster, and younger. He will tell her now why he was the best. He touches his little finger to his eyelid. "The seeing, the true seeing, that is the heart of it."

paragraphs.context: “The first sword of Braavos does not run,” he sang
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya watches Syrio fight the fully armored Ser Meryn with a wooden sword, until his stick is cut in two, and then she runs.
paragraphs.simple: Arya remembers Syrio's words: look with your eyes. She sees the knight head to foot in pale armor, eyes hidden behind his helm, with cruel steel in his hand. Against that stands Syrio in a leather vest with a wooden sword. "Syrio, run," she screams. He sings back, "The first sword of Braavos does not run." He dances away from the knight's cuts, bouncing blows off helm, gauntlet, and gorget. But the fourth cut slices his stick in two. Sobbing, Arya spins and runs.

paragraphs.context: Everything Syrio Forel had ever taught her vanished in a
paragraphs.mainIdea: When the stableboy grabs her, Arya forgets all of Syrio's lessons and kills him with the one lesson Jon gave her: stick him with the pointy end.
paragraphs.simple: The stableboy grabs Arya's arm hard. Everything Syrio ever taught her vanishes in a heartbeat. In her terror, the only lesson she can remember is the very first one Jon Snow gave her. She sticks the boy with the pointy end of Needle, driving the blade upward with wild, hysterical strength. It goes through his jerkin and belly and comes out between his shoulder blades. The boy drops the pitchfork and dies. Arya has killed someone for the first time.

paragraphs.context: Sansa had expected that Ser Boros would escort her to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Crossing the bridge, Sansa sees a body impaled on the iron spikes in the dry moat below.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa expected to be taken to the royal apartments, but Ser Boros leads her out of Maegor's Holdfast. The bridge is down again. Some workmen are lowering a man on ropes into the depths of the dry moat. When Sansa peers down, she sees a body impaled on the huge iron spikes below. She averts her eyes quickly, afraid to ask, afraid to look too long, afraid he might be someone she knows.

paragraphs.context: “It was for love,” Sansa said in a rush. “Father
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa confesses that she told the queen about Ned's plan to leave, because she loved Joffrey and did not want to be sent back to Winterfell.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa rushes to explain. She had been the good, obedient girl, but that morning she felt as wicked as Arya, sneaking away from Septa Mordane and defying her father. She had never done anything so willful before. But she loved Joffrey so much. Ned was going to take her back to Winterfell and marry her to some hedge knight. She told him, but he would not listen. The king frightened her, so she went to the queen instead and poured out her heart. Cersei listened and thanked her sweetly. Then Ser Arys escorted her to a guarded room, and a few hours later the fighting began outside.

paragraphs.context: “She reminds me of the mother, not the father,” Lord
paragraphs.mainIdea: Littlefinger speaks for Sansa, saying she takes after her mother, not her father.
paragraphs.simple: Varys says it is truly said that blood runs truer than oaths. Then Lord Petyr Baelish speaks quietly. "She reminds me of the mother, not the father," he says. "Look at her. The hair, the eyes. She is the very image of Cat at the same age." The queen looks at Sansa, troubled, but Sansa can see kindness in her green eyes.

paragraphs.context: Ghost ran with them for a time and then vanished
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon remembers Old Nan's tales of the Others: cold and dead, hating iron and fire, riding pale dead horses and leading hosts of the slain.
paragraphs.simple: Riding back, Jon remembers the tales Old Nan used to tell them at Winterfell. In the darkness the Others came riding, she used to say, dropping her voice lower and lower. Cold and dead they were, and they hated iron and fire and the touch of the sun, and every living creature with hot blood in its veins. Cities and kingdoms of men all fell before them as they moved south on pale dead horses, leading hosts of the slain. They fed their dead servants on the flesh of human children.

paragraphs.context: “Lord Eddard has been imprisoned. He is charged with treason.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mormont tells Jon that Ned has been imprisoned for treason, accused of plotting to deny the throne to Joffrey.
paragraphs.simple: Mormont tells Jon the grievous news. Lord Eddard has been imprisoned. He is charged with treason. It is said he plotted with Robert's brothers to deny the throne to Prince Joffrey. Jon says at once that it cannot be: his father would never betray the king. Mormont says it is not for them to judge.

paragraphs.context: Jon tried to shout, but his voice was gone. Staggering
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon seizes Mormont's oil lamp and sets the drapes ablaze, remembering that fire kills what steel cannot.
paragraphs.simple: Jon's voice is gone. He staggers up, kicks the crawling arm away, and snatches the lamp from the Old Bear's fingers. The raven caws, "Burn! Burn, burn, burn!" Jon flings the lamp into the drapes he ripped from the window. Oil spews, and the hangings go up in a great whoosh of flame. The heat on his face is sweeter than any kiss Jon has ever known. He grabs a fistful of the burning drapes and whips them at the dead man. "Let it burn," he prays. "Gods, please, please, let it burn." ## Sentence notes

paragraphs.context: And when Lord Umber, who was called the Greatjon by
paragraphs.mainIdea: When the Greatjon threatens to take his men home, Robb threatens to hang him as an oathbreaker, and Grey Wind bites off two of his fingers.
paragraphs.simple: Lord Umber, called the Greatjon, threatens to take his forces home if he is placed behind the Hornwoods or Cerwyns in the order of march. Robb tells him he is welcome to do so. And when they are done with the Lannisters, they will march north, root him out of his keep, and hang him for an oathbreaker. The enraged Greatjon throws a flagon into the fire, knocks men down, and draws a huge greatsword. Robb says one quiet word, and Grey Wind is on him: the Greatjon falls with two fingers bitten off.

paragraphs.context: “Let Maester Luwin ride beyond the Wall,” Osha said. “He’ll
paragraphs.mainIdea: Osha tells Bran about the giants beyond the Wall: ten to thirteen feet tall, fierce, hairy, with bearded wives.
paragraphs.simple: Osha says if Luwin rode beyond the Wall, he would find giants, or they would find him. Her brother killed one: ten feet tall she was, and stunted at that. They can grow to twelve or thirteen feet. They are fierce, all hair and teeth, and the wives have beards like their husbands, so you cannot tell them apart. The women take human men as lovers, and the half-bloods come from them.

paragraphs.context: “Will he now? We’ll see. You tell him this, m’lord.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Osha asks Bran to tell Robb he is marching the wrong way: he should take his swords north, not south.
paragraphs.simple: Osha tells Bran to give Robb a message: he is bound on marching the wrong way. It is north he should be taking his swords. North, not south. Bran promises he will tell him. But that night Robb is feasting with the lords, making the final plans for the march south, and the moment passes.

paragraphs.context: If I were not the blood of the dragon, she
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany admits Vaes Dothrak could be her home, but as the last dragon she cannot forget who she is and what she must do.
paragraphs.simple: Dany thinks wistfully that if she were not the blood of the dragon, Vaes Dothrak could be her home. She is khaleesi, with a strong husband, a swift horse, servants, warriors, and an honored place awaiting her in old age. And in her womb grows a son who will one day bestride the world. That should be enough for any woman, but not for the dragon. With Viserys gone, she is the last, the very last. She is the seed of kings and conquerors. She must not forget.

paragraphs.context: “Yes.” The knight drew out a folded parchment. “A letter
paragraphs.mainIdea: Illyrio's letter reveals that Robert Baratheon offers lands and lordships for the deaths of Dany, her brother, and her child.
paragraphs.simple: Back in her home, Dany asks Jorah if it was the Usurper. "Yes," he says. He shows her a letter to Viserys from Magister Illyrio. Robert Baratheon offers lands and lordships for the death of Dany, or her brother. Dany laughs through a sob: Robert does not know Viserys is already dead. The Usurper owes Drogo a lordship. Jorah adds grimly: the offer is for Dany and the child too.

paragraphs.context: “And to Rhaego son of Drogo, the stallion who will
paragraphs.mainIdea: Drogo swears a great oath: he will sail the wooden horses across the black salt water, kill the men in iron suits, and give the Seven Kingdoms to his unborn son.
paragraphs.simple: When Dany tells Drogo what happened, all laughter stops. Drogo grows very quiet. Then he speaks: the poisoner ran from the moon of his life; better he should run after her. And to Rhaego, the stallion who will mount the world, Drogo pledges a gift: the iron chair his mother's father sat in. He will give him the Seven Kingdoms. He will take his khalasar west, ride the wooden horses across the black salt water as no khal has done before. He will kill the men in iron suits and tear down their stone houses. He will rape their women, take their children as slaves, and bring their broken gods back to Vaes Dothrak. This he vows before the Mother of Mountains.

paragraphs.context: Something in Robb’s tone troubled her. She smoothed out the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn reads Sansa's letter and sees through it: it is Cersei's letter, and the threat is hidden in what Sansa does not say.
paragraphs.simple: Catelyn reads Sansa's letter. Concern gives way to disbelief, then anger, then fear. "This is Cersei's letter, not your sister's," she says. "The real message is in what Sansa does not say. All this about how kindly and gently the Lannisters are treating her… I know the sound of a threat, even whispered. They have Sansa hostage, and they mean to keep her."

paragraphs.context: “I do not know, Robb. What I do know is
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn tells Robb he has no choice but to fight: only if the Lannisters fear his power will Ned and Sansa be safe.
paragraphs.simple: Robb fears the Lannisters will kill Ned and Sansa if he fights. Catelyn says she does not know. But he has no choice. If he goes to King's Landing to swear fealty, he will never be allowed to leave. If he retreats to Winterfell, his lords will lose respect for him, and some may join the Lannisters. Their only hope is that he defeats the foe in the field. If he captures Tywin or the Kingslayer, a trade might be possible. But the heart of it is this: so long as he has power enough that they must fear him, Ned and Sansa should be safe.

paragraphs.context: Robb drew a map across the table, a ragged piece
paragraphs.mainIdea: Robb lays out his plan: march south, then split the host, sending the foot down the kingsroad while the horse crosses the Green Fork at the Twins.
paragraphs.simple: Robb draws a map across the table. Both plans have virtues, but if they swing around Tywin's army, they risk being caught between Tywin and the Kingslayer, and Tywin has more men and more armored horse. The Greatjon says it will not matter if they catch Tywin unprepared, but Robb doubts a man who has fought as many battles as Tywin will be so easily surprised. His plan: leave a small force at Moat Cailin, march south, then split the host in two. The foot continues down the kingsroad while the horsemen cross the Green Fork at the Twins. When Tywin marches north to meet the main host, the riders will be free to hurry down the west bank to Riverrun.

paragraphs.context: Tywin Lannister, Lord of Casterly Rock and Warden of the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion describes his father: hard as a man of twenty, bald by choice, with great golden sidewhiskers and pale green eyes flecked with gold.
paragraphs.simple: Tywin Lannister is in his middle fifties, yet hard as a man of twenty. Even seated, he is tall, with long legs, broad shoulders, a flat stomach. When his golden hair began to recede, he ordered his barber to shave his head; Lord Tywin does not believe in half measures. He shaves his lip and chin too, but keeps his sidewhiskers, two great thickets of wiry golden hair. His eyes are pale green, flecked with gold.

paragraphs.context: His father ignored the sally. “The honor of our House
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin explains that the honor of House Lannister forced him to go to war: no one may shed Lannister blood without punishment.
paragraphs.simple: Tywin ignores Tyrion's joke. The honor of their House was at stake. He had no choice but to ride to war. No man sheds Lannister blood with impunity, without being punished. "Hear Me Roar," Tyrion says, grinning: the Lannister words. He adds that none of his blood was actually shed, though it was close once or twice. Only his guards Morrec and Jyck were killed.

paragraphs.context: “I said nothing of need,” Lord Tywin replied. “My words
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin flatters the clansmen into joining him by saying he needs nothing from them, since even his boldest knights fear the northerners.
paragraphs.simple: When Ulf asks why they need Tywin's promise when they have Tyrion's, Tywin says he spoke of courtesy, nothing more. They need not join him. The men of the winterlands are made of iron and ice, and even his boldest knights fear to face them. Tyrion thinks, "Oh, deftly done," smiling crookedly. Tywin is playing on the clansmen's pride: by saying he does not need them and his knights are afraid, he makes them eager to prove him wrong.

paragraphs.context: Sansa watched as the knight peered up at his new
paragraphs.mainIdea: Barristan recalls his life of service: chosen for the Kingsguard at twenty-three, giving up land and marriage, serving three kings.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa watches the knight peer up at his new king. He looks his years now, for the first time. He says he was chosen for the White Swords in his twenty-third year. It was all he had ever dreamed of. He gave up all claim to his ancestral keep. The girl he was to marry wed his cousin instead. He had no need of land or sons; his life would be lived for the realm. He fought beside the White Bull and Prince Lewyn of Dorne, beside Ser Arthur Dayne, the Sword of the Morning. He served King Aerys, and Aerys's father Jaehaerys before him: three kings.

paragraphs.context: Ser Barristan looked up sharply. “A hall to die in,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Barristan rejects their pity and their gift of lands, strips off his white cloak, and declares he will die a knight.
paragraphs.simple: Varys offers Barristan lands, gold, and men to build a keep by the sea. Barristan looks up sharply. "A hall to die in, and men to bury me. I thank you, my lords… but I spit upon your pity." He undoes the clasps of his cloak, and the heavy white garment falls to the floor. His helmet drops with a clang. "I am a knight," he tells them. He unfastens his breastplate and lets that fall as well. "I shall die a knight."

paragraphs.context: Sansa heard someone gasp. Ser Boros and Ser Meryn moved
paragraphs.mainIdea: Barristan throws his sword at the foot of the throne and leaves, saying Stannis may yet sit on the Iron Throne.
paragraphs.simple: Barristan freezes the other Kingsguard with a look of contempt. "Even now, I could cut through the five of you as easy as a dagger cuts cheese. If you would serve under the Kingslayer, not a one of you is fit to wear the white." He flings his sword at the foot of the Iron Throne. "Here, boy. Melt it down and add it to the others, if you like. Perhaps Lord Stannis will chance to sit on it when he takes your throne." He takes the long way out, his steps ringing against the floor.

paragraphs.context: He could no longer tell the difference between waking and
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ned remembers the tourney at Harrenhal in the year of the false spring: Brandon's laughter, Robert's valor, and young Jaime taking the white cloak.
paragraphs.simple: Ned can no longer tell waking from sleeping. A memory comes, vivid as a dream: the year of the false spring, when he was eighteen, down from the Eyrie to the tourney at Harrenhal. He remembers Brandon's laughter, and Robert's wild valor in the melee, laughing as he unhorsed men left and right. He remembers Jaime Lannister, a golden youth in white armor, kneeling before the king's pavilion to take his Kingsguard vows. All six White Swords were there to welcome their newest brother.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, indeed. Cersei gave him the wineskins, and told him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Varys tells Ned that it was not the wine that killed Robert; it was Ned's mercy in warning Cersei.
paragraphs.simple: Varys confirms that Cersei gave Lancel the wineskins and told him it was Robert's favorite vintage. But a hunter lives a perilous life: if the boar had not killed Robert, it would have been a fall, a snakebite, a stray arrow. The forest is the slaughterhouse of the gods. "It was not wine that killed the king," Varys says. "It was your mercy." By warning Cersei, Ned gave her time to arrange Robert's death. Ned had feared as much. "Gods forgive me."

paragraphs.context: “A boy with an army,” Varys said. “Yet only a
paragraphs.mainIdea: Varys describes Cersei's nightmare: while Tywin fights the Starks, Stannis will land and take Joffrey's head.
paragraphs.simple: Varys says the king's brothers are giving Cersei sleepless nights, Stannis in particular. His claim is the true one, he is a proven battle commander, and he is utterly without mercy. No one knows what Stannis has been doing on Dragonstone, but he has surely gathered swords. Here is Cersei's nightmare: while her father and brother spend their power fighting Starks and Tullys, Lord Stannis will land, proclaim himself king, and cut off her son's curly blond head, and her own as well. Though Varys believes she cares more about the boy.

paragraphs.context: Lord Walder was ninety, a wizened pink weasel with a
paragraphs.mainIdea: Walder Frey is ninety, gouty, and wizened, with a sixteen-year-old eighth wife walking beside his litter.
paragraphs.simple: Lord Walder is ninety, a wizened pink weasel with a bald spotted head, too gouty to stand unassisted. His newest wife, a pale frail girl of sixteen, walks beside his litter when they carry him in. She is the eighth Lady Frey.

paragraphs.context: “They’ll be twenty thousand fresh corpses when Lord Tywin gets
