paragraphs.mainIdea: Walder boasts that he will match Catelyn son for son, and still have eighteen left when hers are dead.
paragraphs.simple: When Catelyn points out her son's twenty thousand men outside his walls, Walder shoots back that they will be twenty thousand fresh corpses when Tywin arrives. He should not try to frighten him. Her husband is in a traitor's cell, her father may be dying, her brother is in chains. What does she have that he should fear? Her son? "I'll match you son for son," he boasts, "and I'll still have eighteen when yours are all dead."

paragraphs.context: The rest was only haggling.
paragraphs.mainIdea: After the talk, the deal is struck, and Catelyn rides out with Frey's sons and a column of pikemen behind her.
paragraphs.simple: "The rest was only haggling." At sunset, the castle gates open, the drawbridge comes down, and Catelyn rides out to rejoin her son. Behind her come four of Walder's sons and his bastard Ronel Rivers, leading a long column of pikemen in blue steel ringmail and silvery grey cloaks. The crossing is granted.

paragraphs.context: “So they will not love,” the old man answered, “for
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aemon explains why the Watch takes no wives: so they will not love, for love is the bane of honor, the death of duty.
paragraphs.simple: Aemon asks Jon if he ever wondered why the men of the Night's Watch take no wives and father no children. Jon shrugs. "So they will not love," the old man answers, "for love is the bane of honor, the death of duty." That does not sound right to Jon, yet he says nothing. The maester is a hundred years old, and it is not Jon's place to contradict him.

paragraphs.context: “A craven can be as brave as any man, when
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aemon tells Jon that duty is easy when it costs nothing; the test comes when a man must choose.
paragraphs.simple: A craven can be as brave as any man, when there is nothing to fear. And we all do our duty, when there is no cost to it. How easy it seems then, to walk the path of honor. Yet soon or late in every man's life comes a day when it is not easy, a day when he must choose." Jon asks if this is his day. Aemon lays a withered hand on his shoulder. "It hurts, boy. Oh, yes. Choosing… it has always hurt. And always will. I know.

paragraphs.context: A toothless smile quivered on the ancient lips. “Only a
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aemon reveals who he is: Aemon Targaryen, son of King Maekar, brother of King Aegon, who gave up the throne to take the black.
paragraphs.simple: Jon asks who he is. Aemon smiles. He is only a maester of the Citadel, bound in service to the Watch; in their order they put aside house names when they take their vows. But his father was Maekar, the First of his Name, and his brother Aegon reigned after him in his stead. His grandfather named him for Prince Aemon the Dragonknight. "Aemon… Targaryen?" Jon can scarcely believe it. "Once," the old man says. "Once." ## Sentence notes

paragraphs.context: Slaves, Dany thought. Khal Drogo would drive them downriver to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany tells herself to be strong: this is war, this is what it looks like, this is the price of the Iron Throne.
paragraphs.simple: Dany thinks of the ten thousand captives as slaves. Drogo will drive them downriver to the towns on Slaver's Bay. She wants to cry, but she tells herself she must be strong. This is war, this is what it looks like, this is the price of the Iron Throne. She is trying to accept what her dream of Westeros will cost.

paragraphs.context: Jorah Mormont spurred his horse closer. “Princess,” he said, “you
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jorah tells Dany she does not understand: the riders shed blood for the khal, and now they claim their reward.
paragraphs.simple: When Dany orders the rape stopped, Jorah rides closer. "Princess," he says, "you have a gentle heart, but you do not understand. This is how it has always been. Those men have shed blood for the khal. Now they claim their reward." He means the Dothraki believe rape is the warriors' rightful prize for fighting.

paragraphs.context: Qotho was ever the cruelest of the bloodriders. It was
paragraphs.mainIdea: Qotho mocks Dany's plan to wed the Lamb women to Dothraki riders, asking if a horse breeds with a sheep.
paragraphs.simple: When Dany says the warriors should take the Lamb women gently as wives and let them bear sons, Qotho laughs. He is ever the cruelest of the bloodriders. "Does the horse breed with the sheep?" he asks. He means the Dothraki are horses and the Lamb Men are sheep: the two should never mix. Something in his tone reminds Dany of Viserys.

paragraphs.context: In the dawn light, the army of Lord Tywin Lannister
paragraphs.mainIdea: At dawn, Tywin's army unfolds like an iron rose, thorns gleaming.
paragraphs.simple: In the dawn light, the army of Lord Tywin Lannister unfolds like an iron rose, thorns gleaming. Tyrion's uncle Kevan leads the center, with archers, pikemen, and men-at-arms around the kingsroad. The right wing is all cavalry, four thousand heavy horse under Ser Addam Marbrand. Tywin himself commands the reserve of five thousand on the hill, watching the battle unfold below.

paragraphs.context: Clegane had no splendor about him; his armor was steel
paragraphs.mainIdea: Gregor orders Tyrion to take the left and hold the river, if he can.
paragraphs.simple: Gregor Clegane has no splendor: dull grey scarred plate with no sigil. He waves a two-handed greatsword about with one hand. "Any man runs, I'll cut him down myself," he roars. When he sees Tyrion: "Imp! Take the left. Hold the river. If you can." Tyrion leads his men to the riverbank: the left of the left. To turn their flank, the Starks would need horses that can run on water.

paragraphs.context: Lord Tywin drained his cup, his face expressionless. “I put
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin admits he placed his worst troops on the left hoping they would break, to lure Robb into a trap.
paragraphs.simple: Tywin drains his cup, expressionless. "I put the least disciplined men on the left, yes. I anticipated that they would break. Robb Stark is a green boy, more like to be brave than wise. I'd hoped that if he saw our left collapse, he might plunge into the gap, eager for a rout. Once he was fully committed, Kevan's pikes would wheel and take him in the flank, driving him into the river while I brought up the reserve." Tyrion was meant to be sacrificed as bait.

paragraphs.context: The sound seemed to go right through Catelyn Stark, and
paragraphs.mainIdea: Grey Wind's howl goes through Catelyn, and she thinks: so this is what death sounds like.
paragraphs.simple: Grey Wind's howl seems to go right through Catelyn, and she shivers. It is a terrible sound, a frightening sound, yet there is music in it too. For a second she feels something like pity for the Lannisters below. "So this is what death sounds like," she thinks. From the far ridge the Greatjon winds his horn in answer, and the trumpets of the Mallisters and Freys blow vengeance.

paragraphs.context: “—I should then be mourning in place of Lord Karstark,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn warns Robb there is no time for grief: they have lopped the head off the snake, but most of the body still surrounds Riverrun.
paragraphs.simple: Catelyn tells Robb his men died protecting their liege lord. He should grieve for them and honor their valor, but not now. He has no time for grief. "You may have lopped the head off the snake, but three quarters of the body is still coiled around my father's castle. We have won a battle, not a war."

paragraphs.context: Khal Drogo reeled in the saddle, tilted slowly, and fell
paragraphs.mainIdea: Khal Drogo reels in the saddle and falls heavily from his horse, while the flies settle on him where he lies.
paragraphs.simple: Dany rides closer and touches Drogo's arm. Khal Drogo reels in the saddle, tilts slowly, and falls heavily from his horse. The flies scatter for a heartbeat, then circle back to settle on him where he lies. "No," Dany says, reining up. Heedless of her belly, she scrambles off her silver and runs to him.

paragraphs.context: Trembling, her eyes full of sudden tears, Dany turned away
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany knows what the fall means: a khal who cannot ride cannot rule, and Drogo has fallen from his horse.
paragraphs.simple: Dany knows they cannot keep the fall secret, and she knows what it means. A khal who cannot ride cannot rule, and Drogo has fallen from his horse. Among the Dothraki, a khal's power is his strength in the saddle. A khal who falls is finished. She must not despair. "We must bathe him," she says stubbornly.

paragraphs.context: “It is not a matter of gold or horses. This
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mirri warns that this is bloodmagic: only death can pay for life, though not Dany's death.
paragraphs.simple: Mirri warns there is a price. Dany offers gold and horses, whatever she likes. "It is not a matter of gold or horses. This is bloodmagic, lady. Only death may pay for life." "Death?" Dany wraps her arms around herself. "My death?" She tells herself she would die for him; her brother Rhaegar died for the woman he loved. "No," Mirri promises. "Not your death, Khaleesi." Trembling with relief, Dany says, "Do it."

paragraphs.context: Arya glanced warily behind her. Two of the City Watch
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya fears the City Watch — the "gold cloaks" — who have thrown in with the Lannisters; the heads of the executed rot on the red walls.
paragraphs.simple: The City Watch wear heavy gold wool cloaks, black mail, boots, and gloves. Their commander has been raised to a lord and given lands and a council seat — the gold cloaks have thrown in with the Lannisters. Arya keeps away from the castle, but even from a distance she can see heads rotting atop the high red walls. Flocks of crows squabble over each head, thick as flies. The sight of the gold cloaks ties her stomach in knots.

paragraphs.context: A thousand voices were screaming, but Arya never heard them.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Joffrey sets aside the pleas for mercy and orders Ser Ilyn Payne to bring him Ned's head.
paragraphs.simple: A thousand voices scream, but Arya never hears them. Joffrey steps out from behind his Kingsguard's shields. "My mother bids me let Lord Eddard take the black, and Lady Sansa has begged mercy for her father." He looks at Sansa and smiles — and for a moment Arya thinks the gods have heard her prayer. Then he turns back to the crowd: "But they have the soft hearts of women. So long as I am your king, treason shall never go unpunished. Ser Ilyn, bring me his head!"

paragraphs.context: Ser Ilyn drew a two-handed greatsword from the scabbard on
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ser Ilyn draws a greatsword — and Arya realizes with horror that it is Ice, her father's own sword.
paragraphs.simple: Ser Ilyn draws a two-handed greatsword from the scabbard on his back. As he lifts the blade, sunlight ripples down the dark metal, glinting off an edge sharper than any razor. Ice, she thinks — he has Ice! Her tears stream down her face, blinding her. The executioner will kill her father with the Stark sword itself.

paragraphs.context: “But some twelve thousand years ago, the First Men appeared
paragraphs.mainIdea: The First Men came with bronze and horses, warred with the children for centuries, until both sides forged the Pact on the Isle of Faces.
paragraphs.simple: Some twelve thousand years ago, the First Men came from the east, crossing the Broken Arm of Dorne before it was broken. They came with bronze swords and horses — no horse had ever been seen on this side of the narrow sea. The wars went on until the earth ran red with blood, but more children than men, for wood and stone and obsidian make a poor match for bronze. Finally the wise of both races prevailed, and on the Isle of Faces they forged the Pact: the First Men took the open lands, the deep woods stayed the children's forever, and no more weirwoods were to be put to the axe.

paragraphs.context: “The Andals were the first, a race of tall, fair-haired
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Andals came with steel and the new gods, slaughtered the children, and drove them north beyond the Wall.
paragraphs.simple: Many centuries later, other peoples crossed the narrow sea. The Andals were the first: tall, fair-haired warriors with steel and fire and the seven-pointed star of the new gods on their chests. The wars lasted hundreds of years, but the six southron kingdoms all fell. Only in the North, where the King in the North threw back every army at the Neck, did the rule of the First Men endure. The Andals burnt the weirwood groves, slaughtered the children where they found them, and proclaimed the triumph of the Seven. So the children fled north — and then the wolves began to howl.

paragraphs.context: Maester Luwin looked up at them numbly, a small grey
paragraphs.mainIdea: The raven brings the news: Luwin's grief tells Bran they need a stonecarver who knew Ned's likeness — Ned is dead.
paragraphs.simple: Luwin stares at the black bird, then rises slow as a sleepwalker and takes the letter from its leg. Bran shivers. "What is it?" Osha answers: "You know what it is, boy." Luwin looks up, a small grey man with blood on his sleeve and tears in his eyes. "My lords," he says to the sons, in a voice gone hoarse and shrunken, "we… we shall need to find a stonecarver who knew his likeness well…" A stonecarver, to carve Ned's statue for the crypts. ## Sentence notes

paragraphs.context: “He wants you to smile and smell sweet and be
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Hound tells Sansa what Joffrey wants from her: her pretty courtesies, her love — and her fear.
paragraphs.simple: The Hound lingers and tells her: "Save yourself some pain, girl, and give him what he wants." When she begs to know what he wants, he rasps: "He wants you to smile and smell sweet and be his lady love. He wants to hear you recite all your pretty little words the way the septa taught you. He wants you to love him… and fear him." After he leaves, Sansa sinks down and stares at the wall until her maids come.

paragraphs.context: Frog-faced Lord Slynt sat at the end of the council
paragraphs.mainIdea: Watching Janos Slynt, Sansa wishes a hero would kill him — then remembers Littlefinger's lesson: life is not a song, and in life the monsters win.
paragraphs.simple: Frog-faced Lord Slynt sits nodding approval at every sentence. Sansa stares at his ugly face, remembering how he threw down her father for Ser Ilyn to behead, wishing some hero would throw him down and cut off his head. But a voice inside her whispers, "There are no heroes." She remembers Littlefinger's words: "Life is not a song, sweetling. You may learn that one day to your sorrow." In life, the monsters win, she tells herself — and hears the Hound's cold rasp: "Save yourself some pain, girl, and give him what he wants."

paragraphs.context: The outer parapet came up to her chin, but along
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa calculates that one shove would send Joffrey over the inner edge — seventy feet down — even if she went with him.
paragraphs.simple: The outer parapet comes up to her chin, but along the inner edge of the walk is nothing, nothing but a long plunge to the bailey seventy or eighty feet below. "All it would take was a shove," she tells herself. He is standing right there, right there, smirking at her with those fat wormlips. "You could do it," she tells herself. "You could. Do it right now. It wouldn't even matter if she went over with him. It wouldn't matter at all."

paragraphs.context: “No,” Mirri Maz Duur said. “That was a lie you
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mirri tells Dany the price was never the horse: Dany knew the price was her child, and lied to herself.
paragraphs.simple: Dany says, "You warned me that only death could pay for life. I thought you meant the horse." "No," Mirri says. "That was a lie you told yourself. You knew the price." "Had she? Had she? If I look back I am lost." Dany lists the dead: the horse, her child, Quaro and Qotho, Haggo and Cohollo. "The price was paid and paid and paid. Where is Khal Drogo? Show me what I bought with my son's life."

paragraphs.context: “When the sun rises in the west and sets in
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mirri answers when Drogo will be as he was: when impossible things happen — the sun rising in the west, seas going dry, Dany bearing a living child.
paragraphs.simple: "When will he be as he was?" Dany demands. "When the sun rises in the west and sets in the east," Mirri says. "When the seas go dry and mountains blow in the wind like leaves. When your womb quickens again, and you bear a living child. Then he will return, and not before." It is a prophecy of impossibilities — a cruel way of saying never.

paragraphs.context: She knelt, kissed Drogo on the lips, and pressed the
paragraphs.mainIdea: At dawn, knowing Drogo is truly lost, Dany smothers him with a cushion — a mercy killing, her last act of love.
paragraphs.simple: When the bleak dawn breaks, Dany knows he is truly lost to her. She finds a cushion of soft silk stuffed with feathers and clutches it to her breasts as she walks back out to Drogo. "If I look back I am lost." It hurts even to walk. She kneels, kisses Drogo on the lips, and presses the cushion down across his face. She ends his empty life rather than let him linger as a husk. ## Sentence notes

paragraphs.context: “Peace?” Tyrion swirled his wine thoughtfully, took a deep draft,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion smashes his cup to show what "peace" is worth now: Joffrey broke it beyond repair when he took Ned's head.
paragraphs.simple: When Ser Harys urges suing for peace, Tyrion swirls his wine, drinks deep, and hurls the empty cup to the floor, where it shatters into a thousand pieces. "There's your peace, Ser Harys. My sweet nephew broke it for good and all when he decided to ornament the Red Keep with Lord Eddard's head. You'll have an easier time drinking wine from that cup than you will convincing Robb Stark to make peace now. He's winning… or hadn't you noticed?"

paragraphs.context: “Let her say what she likes. Her son needs to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin rails at Joffrey's follies: making Janos Slynt a lord with a bloody spear for his sigil, dismissing Barristan Selmy.
paragraphs.simple: Tywin blames the jackanapes on the council — Petyr, Pycelle, Varys — for Joffrey's follies. Whose notion was it to make Janos Slynt a lord? The man's father was a butcher, and they grant him Harrenhal — "Harrenhal, that was the seat of kings! I am told he took a bloody spear for his sigil. A bloody cleaver would have been my choice." And dismissing Selmy — where was the sense? "The name of Barristan the Bold still has meaning in the realm. He lent honor to any man he served. Can anyone say the same of the Hound? You feed your dog bones under the table, you do not seat him beside you on the high bench."

paragraphs.context: Lord Tywin rose abruptly. “You are my son.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: When Tyrion asks "Why me?", Tywin answers only "You are my son" — and Tyrion understands: Tywin has given Jaime up for lost.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion asks why him — why not Kevan, or Addam, or a bigger man? Tywin rises abruptly. "You are my son." That is when Tyrion knows. "You have given him up for lost," he thinks. "You bloody bastard, you think Jaime's good as dead, so I'm all you have left." Tyrion wants to slap him, to spit in his face, to cut the heart out of him and see if it is made of old hard gold, as the smallfolk say. Yet he sits there, silent and still.

paragraphs.context: “We’re your brothers now,” Grenn said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: When Jon says he belongs with Robb, Grenn answers: "We're your brothers now" — the Watch is his family.
paragraphs.simple: I belong with my brother," Jon says. "We're your brothers now," Grenn says. "They'll cut off your head if they catch you, you know," Toad adds nervously. "I'm no oathbreaker. I said the words and I meant them." "So did I," Jon tells them. "Don't you understand? They murdered my father. It's war, my brother Robb is fighting in the riverlands—" "We know," Pyp says solemnly. "Sam told us everything." "We're sorry about your father, but it doesn't matter. Once you say the words, you can't leave, no matter what.

paragraphs.context: “It’s not,” Mormont told him. “Gods save us, boy, you’re
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mormont's challenge: when dead men hunt in the night, does it matter who sits the Iron Throne?
paragraphs.simple: "Do you think your brother's war is more important than ours?" the old man barks. The raven flaps its wings: "War, war, war, war." "It's not," Mormont tells him. "Gods save us, boy, you're not blind and you're not stupid. When dead men come hunting in the night, do you think it matters who sits the Iron Throne?" "No." Jon had not thought of it that way.

paragraphs.context: “You heard me. I mean to find Ben Stark, alive
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mormont demands an answer now: is Jon a brother of the Night's Watch, or only a bastard boy who wants to play at war?
paragraphs.simple: Mormont points his dagger at Jon's chest. "By custom, the Lord Commander's steward is his squire as well… but I do not care to wake every dawn wondering if you've run off again. So I will have an answer from you, Lord Snow, and I will have it now. Are you a brother of the Night's Watch… or only a bastard boy who wants to play at war?" Jon straightens. "Forgive me, Father. Robb, Arya, Bran… forgive me, I cannot help you. He has the truth of it. This is my place." "I am… yours, my lord. Your man. I swear it. I will not run again." ## Sentence notes

paragraphs.context: “Renly is crowned,” said Marq Piper. “Highgarden and Storm’s End
paragraphs.mainIdea: Piper argues for Renly: with five or six great houses behind him, they'd have every Lannister head on a pike within the year.
paragraphs.simple: "Renly is crowned," says Marq Piper. "Highgarden and Storm's End support his claim, and the Dornishmen will not be laggardly. If Winterfell and Riverrun add their strength to his, he will have five of the seven great houses behind him. Six, if the Arryns bestir themselves! Six against the Rock! My lords, within the year, we will have all their heads on pikes — the queen and the boy king, Lord Tywin, the Imp, the Kingslayer, Ser Kevan, all of them! That is what we shall win if we join with King Renly. What does Lord Stannis have against that, that we should cast it all aside?" "The right," says Robb stubbornly.

paragraphs.context: The Greatjon bellowed his approval, and other men added their
paragraphs.mainIdea: When Robb lays his sword on the table as "the only peace," Catelyn answers: if that sword could bring Ned back, she'd never let him sheathe it — but it can't.
paragraphs.simple: Robb unsheathes his longsword and lays it on the table. "This is the only peace I have for Lannisters." The Greatjon bellows approval. Catelyn waits for quiet. "My lords, Lord Eddard was your liege, but I shared his bed and bore his children. Do you think I love him any less than you? Robb, if that sword could bring him back, I should never let you sheathe it until Ned stood at my side once more… but he is gone, and a hundred Whispering Woods will not change that. Must we have more deaths still?"

paragraphs.context: “MY LORDS!” he shouted, his voice booming off the rafters.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Greatjon rejects both southern kings, draws his greatsword, and kneels to Robb: "The King in the North!"
paragraphs.simple: "MY LORDS!" the Greatjon shouts, his voice booming off the rafters. "Here is what I say to these two kings!" He spits. "Renly Baratheon is nothing to me, nor Stannis neither. Why should they rule over me and mine, from some flowery seat in Highgarden or Dorne? What do they know of the Wall or the wolfswood or the barrows of the First Men? Even their gods are wrong. The Others take the Lannisters too, I've had a bellyful of them." He draws his immense two-handed greatsword. "Why shouldn't we rule ourselves again? It was the dragons we married, and the dragons are all dead!" He points at Robb. "There sits the only king I mean to bow my knee to, m'lords. The King in the North!" And he kneels, and lays his sword at her son's feet.

paragraphs.context: The godswife did not cry out as they dragged her
paragraphs.mainIdea: As they stake Mirri to the pyre, Dany thanks her for her lessons: it is not her screams Dany wants, only her life — only death can pay for life.
paragraphs.simple: The godswife does not cry out as they drag her to the pyre and stake her down amidst Drogo's treasures. Dany pours the oil over the woman's head herself. "I thank you, Mirri Maz Duur," she says, "for the lessons you have taught me." "You will not hear me scream," Mirri responds. "I will," Dany says, "but it is not your screams I want, only your life. I remember what you told me. Only death can pay for life." For the first time, fear replaces contempt in the maegi's eyes.

paragraphs.context: She could smell the odor of burning flesh, no different
paragraphs.mainIdea: As the pyre roars, Dany stands her ground while all others retreat: she is the blood of the dragon, and the fire is in her.
paragraphs.simple: She can smell burning flesh, no different than horseflesh roasting in a firepit. The pyre roars like some great beast, drowning out Mirri's screaming, sending long tongues of flame to lick the belly of the night. As the smoke thickens, the Dothraki back away, coughing. The heat beats at the air with great red wings, driving the Dothraki back, driving off even Mormont — but Dany stands her ground. She is the blood of the dragon, and the fire is in her.

paragraphs.context: The cream-and-gold dragon was suckling at her left breast, the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Three newborn dragons cling to Dany: cream-and-gold and green-and-bronze suckling at her breasts, black-and-scarlet draped across her shoulders.
paragraphs.simple: The cream-and-gold dragon is suckling at her left breast, the green-and-bronze at the right. Her arms cradle them close. The black-and-scarlet beast is draped across her shoulders, its long sinuous neck coiled under her chin. When it sees Jorah, it raises its head and looks at him with eyes as red as coals.

paragraphs.context: The youngest of the Great Houses, born during the Wars
paragraphs.mainIdea: House Baratheon is the youngest Great House: founded by Orys Baratheon, rumored bastard brother of Aegon the Conqueror, who won the Stormlands by killing the last Storm King.
paragraphs.simple: The Baratheons are the youngest of the Great Houses, born during the Wars of Conquest. Their founder, Orys Baratheon, was rumored to be Aegon the Dragon's bastard brother. Orys rose to become one of Aegon's fiercest commanders. When he defeated and slew Argilac the Arrogant, the last Storm King, Aegon rewarded him with Argilac's castle, lands, and daughter. Orys married the girl and adopted the banner, honors, and words of her line — which is why the Baratheon sigil is a crowned stag and their words are "Ours is the Fury." # Draft notes - ch075 (House Stark) ## Paragraph notes

paragraphs.context: The Starks trace their descent from Brandon the Builder and
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Starks descend from Brandon the Builder and ruled as Kings in the North for thousands of years until Torrhen Stark knelt to Aegon rather than fight.
paragraphs.simple: The Starks trace their descent from Brandon the Builder and the ancient Kings of Winter. For thousands of years, they ruled from Winterfell as Kings in the North — until Torrhen Stark, the King Who Knelt, chose to swear fealty to Aegon the Dragon rather than give battle. That is why the Starks are Wardens of the North now, not kings. # Draft notes - ch076 (House Lannister) ## Paragraph notes

paragraphs.context: Fair-haired, tall, and handsome, the Lannisters are the blood of
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Lannisters descend from Andal adventurers and, through the female line, from the legendary trickster Lann the Clever; Casterly Rock's gold made them the richest Great House.
paragraphs.simple: Fair-haired, tall, and handsome, the Lannisters are the blood of Andal adventurers who carved out a mighty kingdom in the western hills. Through the female line they claim descent from Lann the Clever, the legendary trickster of the Age of Heroes. The gold of Casterly Rock and the Golden Tooth has made them the wealthiest of the Great Houses. # Draft notes - ch077 (House Arryn) ## Paragraph notes

paragraphs.context: The Arryns are descended from the Kings of Mountain and
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Arryns descend from the Kings of Mountain and Vale, among the oldest and purest Andal lines; their sigil is the moon-and-falcon, their words "As High As Honor."
paragraphs.simple: The Arryns are descended from the Kings of Mountain and Vale, one of the oldest and purest lines of Andal nobility. Their sigil is the moon-and-falcon, white, upon a sky blue field. The Arryn words are "As High As Honor." # Draft notes - ch078 (House Tully) ## Paragraph notes

paragraphs.context: The Tullys never reigned as kings, though they held rich
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Tullys were never kings; during the Conquest the riverlands belonged to Harren the Black, whose line had seized the Trident from the Storm Kings.
paragraphs.simple: The Tullys never reigned as kings, though they held rich lands and Riverrun for a thousand years. During the Wars of Conquest, the riverlands belonged to Harren the Black, King of the Isles. Harren's grandfather, King Harwyn Hardhand, had taken the Trident from Arrec the Storm King, whose ancestors had conquered all the way to the Neck three hundred years earlier, slaying the last of the old River Kings. # Draft notes - ch079 (House Tyrell) ## Paragraph notes

paragraphs.context: The Tyrells rose to power as stewards to the Kings
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Tyrells were stewards to the Kings of the Reach until the last king died on the Field of Fire; the steward surrendered to Aegon and was granted Highgarden.
paragraphs.simple: The Tyrells rose to power as stewards to the Kings of the Reach — servants who ran the castle for their kings. Through the female line, they claim descent from Garth Greenhand, gardener king of the First Men, who wore a crown of vines and flowers. When King Mern, last of the old line, perished on the Field of Fire, his steward Harlen Tyrell surrendered Highgarden to Aegon Targaryen, pledging fealty. Aegon granted him the castle and dominion over the Reach. # Draft notes - ch080 (House Greyjoy) ## Paragraph notes

paragraphs.context: The Greyjoys of Pyke claim descent from the Grey King
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Greyjoys claim descent from the legendary Grey King, who ruled the western isles and the sea itself and took a mermaid to wife.
paragraphs.simple: The Greyjoys of Pyke claim descent from the Grey King of the Age of Heroes. Legend says the Grey King ruled not only the western isles but the sea itself, and took a mermaid to wife. # Draft notes - ch081 (House Martell) ## Paragraph notes

paragraphs.context: Nymeria, the warrior queen of the Rhoyne, brought her ten
paragraphs.mainIdea: The warrior queen Nymeria brought ten thousand ships to Dorne and married Mors Martell, making him ruler of all Dorne; Dornish rulers are "Princes," and inheritance goes to the eldest child regardless of sex.
paragraphs.simple: Nymeria, the warrior queen of the Rhoyne, brought her ten thousand ships to land in Dorne and took Lord Mors Martell to husband. With her help, he vanquished his rivals to rule all Dorne. The Rhoynar influence remains strong. Thus Dornish rulers style themselves "Prince" rather than "King." Under Dornish law, lands and titles pass to the eldest child, not the eldest male. # Draft notes - ch082 (House Targaryen) ## Paragraph notes

paragraphs.context: The Targaryens are the blood of the dragon, descended from
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Targaryens descend from the dragonlords of Valyria, marked by their striking, almost inhuman beauty: violet eyes and silver-gold hair.
paragraphs.simple: The Targaryens are the blood of the dragon, descended from the high lords of the ancient Freehold of Valyria. Their heritage shows in a striking — some say inhuman — beauty, with lilac or indigo or violet eyes and hair of silver-gold or platinum white.

sentences.context: Never believe anything you hear at a woman’s tit.
sentences.simple: Do not trust gossip you hear from women.
sentences.grammar: An old saying (proverb) used as a rude dismissal; Royce is mocking both Will's mother and the idea of learning from the dead.

sentences.context: It is hard to take orders from a man you laughed at in your cups, Will reflected as he sat shivering atop his garron.
sentences.simple: It is hard to obey a man you once mocked while drinking.
sentences.grammar: 'In your cups' is an idiom meaning 'while drunk'; the sentence explains why Will and Gared disrespect Royce — they laughed at him over wine in the barracks.

sentences.context: The Others take his eyes,” he swore.
sentences.simple: Damn his eyes! (a northern curse).
sentences.grammar: 'The Others take X' is a common northern oath, like saying 'the devil take him' — it calls on the inhuman enemy beyond the Wall as a curse.

sentences.context: Even Maester Pycelle was helpless, but he brought the milk of the poppy, so Jon did not linger long in pain.
sentences.simple: Even the king's healer could not save him, but he gave Jon a strong painkilling drug, so Jon died quickly without suffering long.
sentences.grammar: 'Milk of the poppy' is the book's name for an opium-like sedative; 'linger' here means to remain alive in suffering.

sentences.context: Viserys lived for that day. All that Daenerys wanted back was the big house with the red door, the lemon tree outside her window, the childhood she had never known.
sentences.simple: Viserys lived only for the day he would win back the throne. All Dany wanted was the little house with the red door, the lemon tree, and the childhood she never had.
sentences.grammar: A parallel contrast in three beats: his dream is a kingdom, hers is a home — the repetition of 'the' items builds her small, human wish against his grand obsession.

sentences.context: What the king dreams,” he said, “the Hand builds.”
sentences.simple: The king imagines things; the Hand has to make them real.
sentences.grammar: A compact proverb in parallel structure (dream/build) that defines the Hand's role: all the work, none of the glory.

sentences.context: They say it grows so cold up here in winter that a man’s laughter freezes in his throat and chokes him to death,” Ned said evenly.
sentences.simple: People say northern winters are so cold that if you laugh, the laugh freezes in your throat and kills you. Maybe that is why Starks are so humorless.
sentences.grammar: Ned's deadpan joke: he answers Robert's demand for a smile with a mock-serious folk saying, using absurd literalism to dodge the order with northern dignity.

sentences.context: There were times—not many, but a few—when Jon Snow was glad he was a bastard.
sentences.simple: Rarely, but sometimes, Jon was actually glad to be a bastard.
sentences.grammar: An ironic opening: the dashes ('not many, but a few') undercut the claim even as he makes it — tonight he can drink freely because no one watches a bastard, which is a small freedom bought with a large shame.

sentences.context: Our wife is duty. Our mistress is honor.
sentences.simple: Duty is our wife; honor is our lover.
sentences.grammar: A parallel metaphor defining the Night's Watch vow: a brother gives up real marriage and family, and takes duty and honor as his only lifelong partners.

sentences.context: My mother died birthing me, and he’s never been sure.”
sentences.simple: My mother died giving birth to me, and my father has never been sure I am truly his son.
sentences.grammar: Devastating understatement: 'never been sure' quietly means Lord Tywin suspects Tyrion may not be his child at all — the dwarf delivers his deepest wound as a dry joke.

sentences.context: There must always be a Stark in Winterfell.
sentences.simple: A Stark must always remain at Winterfell.
sentences.grammar: An ancient Stark maxim stated as law: the castle and the North need their lord's blood present, so Catelyn must stay behind to rule while Ned goes south.

sentences.context: I have to go shoe a horse,” she said sweetly, taking a brief satisfaction in the shock on the septa’s face.
sentences.simple: I have to go put horseshoes on a horse, Arya said politely, enjoying the shock on the septa's face.
sentences.grammar: A pun and a rebellion in one: 'shoe' (to fit a horseshoe) sounds like 'sew' (needlework) — Arya answers the sewing lesson with a blacksmith's job, then flees.

sentences.context: Bastards are not allowed to damage young princes,” he said. “Any bruises they take in the practice yard must come from trueborn swords.”
sentences.simple: A bastard is not allowed to hurt a prince. Any bruises the princes get must come from legitimate-born boys.
sentences.grammar: Jon states a brutal social rule as dry fact, with bitter precision: his skill with a sword is useless because his birth disqualifies him from even touching royalty.

sentences.context: Girls get the arms but not the swords. Bastards get the swords but not the arms.
sentences.simple: Girls get the family crest but not the weapons. Bastards get the weapons but not the family crest.
sentences.grammar: A perfectly balanced aphorism ('arms' means both heraldic arms and weapons): Jon sums up the whole feudal order — everyone gets half of what they need — in two short clauses.

sentences.context: The things I do for love,” he said with loathing. He gave Bran a shove.
sentences.simple: The things I do for love, he said with disgust. Then he pushed Bran out the window.
sentences.grammar: Bitter irony: the tender phrase 'the things I do for love' is spoken with loathing as the excuse for murdering a child — love here means his forbidden love for his sister, which he protects by killing.

sentences.context: I hope the boy does wake. I would be most interested to hear what he might have to say.
sentences.simple: I hope the boy wakes up. I would be very interested to hear what he has to say.
sentences.grammar: A loaded pleasantry: Tyrion pointedly implies Bran might have something to tell about his fall — and Jaime's smile 'curdling like sour milk' shows he caught the threat exactly.

sentences.context: Sometimes prayers are answered.
sentences.simple: Sometimes the gods do answer prayers.
sentences.grammar: A common saying turned horrific: Catelyn means her prayer for Bran to stay home was granted — through his fall — so the comfort of the proverb becomes an accusation against herself.

sentences.context: It should have been you,” she told him.
sentences.simple: You should have been the one who fell, she told him.
sentences.grammar: Five words with no verb of wishing needed: the bare 'should have been' makes it a cold statement of preference — Jon, the bastard, was the expendable child.

sentences.context: First lesson,” Jon said. “Stick them with the pointy end.”
sentences.simple: Here is your first lesson, Jon said. Stab them with the sharp end.
sentences.grammar: Deliberate comic understatement as teaching: the most obvious fact about a sword, stated deadpan, becomes the beloved catchphrase of Arya's whole story.

sentences.context: A Dothraki wedding without at least three deaths is deemed a dull affair,” he had said.
sentences.simple: A Dothraki wedding with fewer than three deaths is considered boring.
sentences.grammar: 'Is deemed' (is considered/judged) states a cultural rule as dry fact — the understatement makes the casual violence more shocking, not less.

sentences.context: As they were bound to Aerys Targaryen’s,” Ned pointed out.
sentences.simple: Just as his life, fortune, and honor were once bound to King Aerys Targaryen's — the king he murdered.
sentences.grammar: Ned's quietest and deadliest line: five words that demolish Robert's trust in Jaime by reminding him that oaths did not stop Jaime last time.

sentences.context: Have no fear, Stark. I was only keeping it warm for our friend Robert.
sentences.simple: Do not be afraid, Stark. I was only keeping the throne warm for our friend Robert.
sentences.grammar: Jaime's insolent joke on being caught sitting the Iron Throne: 'keeping it warm' treats treason as a favor, and the casual 'our friend Robert' claims the new king as an accomplice.

sentences.context: a mind needs books as a sword needs a whetstone, if it is to keep its edge.”
sentences.simple: A mind needs books the way a sword needs a sharpening stone, to stay sharp.
sentences.grammar: A parallel simile (mind/sword, books/whetstone): the comparison makes abstract intellect concrete through the familiar image of maintaining a blade.

sentences.context: Maybe he thought you were a grumkin.
sentences.simple: Maybe Ghost thought you were a grumkin (a fairy-tale monster).
sentences.grammar: Jon's deadpan joke defuses the tension: after Tyrion mocked the Watch for guarding against imaginary monsters, Jon pretends the wolf attacked him for the same reason — and Tyrion's snorting laugh seals their friendship.

sentences.context: It’s good to know my son’s life was not sold cheaply,” Catelyn said bitterly.
sentences.simple: It is good to know my son's life was not sold cheaply.
sentences.grammar: Bitter irony: learning the killer was paid ninety silver stags, Catelyn pretends to take comfort in the high price — the sarcasm barely covers a mother's fury.

sentences.context: I do not think Bran fell from that tower,” she said into the stillness. “I think he was thrown.”
sentences.simple: I do not think Bran fell from that tower. I think someone threw him.
sentences.grammar: The passive 'was thrown' (with the thrower unnamed) lands like a hammer blow: in six words Catelyn turns an accident into attempted murder.

sentences.context: Aerys Targaryen had his tongue ripped out with hot pincers.
sentences.simple: The Mad King Aerys had his tongue torn out with red-hot metal tools.
sentences.grammar: Joffrey delivers the horror flatly, as gossip: the passive construction ('had his tongue ripped out') makes the mutilation sound like a routine royal punishment — which, under Aerys, it was.

sentences.context: Then go,” he spit at her. “And don’t touch me.”
sentences.simple: Then go, he spat at her. And do not touch me.
sentences.grammar: 'Spit' as a speech verb (not 'said') shows pure contempt: the romantic day ends with the prince's mask off — loathing instead of love — in six brutal words.

sentences.context: At least have the courage to do it yourself.
sentences.simple: At least be brave enough to kill her yourself.
sentences.grammar: A conditional challenge: Ned turns Robert's own authority against him — a king who orders death but will not face it is a coward, and the short sentence leaves no room to hide.

sentences.context: He ran.” He looked at Ned’s face and laughed. “But not very fast.”
sentences.simple: He ran. But not very fast.
sentences.grammar: Two flat sentences as a confession of murder: the Hound states the chase and the kill as a joke about the victim's speed, and the casual cruelty is the horror.

sentences.context: Every flight begins with a fall, the crow said.
sentences.simple: Every flight begins with a fall.
sentences.grammar: The crow's paradox: Bran's literal fall from the tower is also the beginning of his new power — destruction and awakening in one line.

sentences.context: Because winter is coming.
sentences.simple: Because winter is coming.
sentences.grammar: The Stark words returned as prophecy: the crow gives Bran his reason to live — not comfort, but warning. The family motto is the dream's final answer.

sentences.context: His name is Summer,” he said.
sentences.simple: His name is Summer, Bran said.
sentences.grammar: Bran's first waking words name his wolf 'Summer' — after dreaming of winter's coming, he names his protector for the season that must be held onto; hope as defiance.

sentences.context: He was always clever, even as a boy, but it is one thing to be clever and another to be wise.
sentences.simple: He was always clever, even as a boy — but being clever and being wise are two different things.
sentences.grammar: A compact distinction that defines Littlefinger: 'clever' is quickness of mind; 'wise' is judgment about how to use it — Catelyn doubts he has the second.

sentences.context: The Imp,” said Littlefinger as Lord Varys watched her face. “Tyrion Lannister.”
sentences.simple: The Imp won it, Littlefinger said — while Varys watched her face. Tyrion Lannister.
sentences.grammar: The chapter's cliffhanger in three beats: the nickname, the watching spymaster, the full name — each short phrase lands harder for being separated.

sentences.context: You’re a Snow, not a Stark. You’re a bastard and a bully.”
sentences.simple: You are a Snow, not a Stark. You are a bastard and a bully.
sentences.grammar: Three hammer-blow labels in parallel: Noye strips Jon of the Stark name he clings to, then names his birth and his behavior — each clause shorter and harder than the last.

sentences.context: If they want to give you a name, take it, make it your own. Then they can’t hurt you with it anymore.”
sentences.simple: If they want to give you a mocking name, take it and make it yours. Then they can never hurt you with it.
sentences.grammar: Tyrion's rule of names in three imperatives (take/make): owning an insult disarms it — the same philosophy he gave Jon at Winterfell, now applied to 'Lord Snow.'

sentences.context: Winter is coming, and when the Long Night falls, only the Night’s Watch will stand between the realm and the darkness that sweeps from the north.
sentences.simple: Winter is coming, and when the Long Night falls, only the Night's Watch will stand between the kingdom and the darkness sweeping down from the north.
sentences.grammar: Mormont's apocalyptic warning in balanced clauses: the Stark words ('Winter is coming') fused with the ancient Long Night myth — the realm's last shield is a dying order of criminals and boys.

sentences.context: All men are made of water, do you know this? When you pierce them, the water leaks out and they die.
sentences.simple: All men are made of water, do you know that? When you pierce them, the water leaks out and they die.
sentences.grammar: Syrio's water-dance philosophy in two flat statements: the body reduced to a waterskin — piercing it is not heroism but hydraulics — which is why the bravo's style is swift and sudden, not hacking and hammering.

sentences.context: The seed is strong, he said.
sentences.simple: The seed is strong, he said.
sentences.grammar: Jon Arryn's dying whisper, cryptic but central: 'seed' means lineage/offspring — the dying Hand was trying to say something about bloodlines and inheritance, the clue Ned will spend the book chasing.

sentences.context: Think the white walkers will care if you have a hostage?
sentences.simple: Do you think the white walkers will care whether you have a hostage?
sentences.grammar: A rhetorical question that reveals the wildlings' true motive: they are not raiding south for plunder but fleeing north from the white walkers — and no hostage will stop the dead.

sentences.context: What do the Stone Crows do, but hide behind rocks and shiver with fear as the knights of the Vale ride by?
sentences.simple: All the Stone Crows ever do is hide behind rocks and tremble with fear when the Vale knights ride past.
sentences.grammar: Rhetorical question used as a taunt; "but" after "do" means "except". # Draft notes - ch044 ## Paragraph notes

sentences.context: he’d taken care to see that he rode under cover of night, without banners, in the guise of a common brigand
sentences.simple: Tywin made sure Gregor attacked at night without banners, looking like an ordinary robber.
sentences.grammar: "in the guise of" means "disguised as"; three parallel phrases describe Gregor's cover. # Draft notes - ch045 ## Paragraph notes

sentences.context: Life is not a song, sweetling. You may learn that one day to your sorrow.
sentences.simple: Real life is not like the romantic stories you love, and you may learn that painfully one day.
sentences.grammar: "to your sorrow" means "in a way that brings you sorrow"; "sweetling" is a term of endearment Littlefinger uses mockingly.

sentences.context: When you play the game of thrones, you win or you die.
sentences.simple: When you play the game of thrones, you either win or you die.
sentences.grammar: A famous compressed saying; "the game of thrones" means the struggle for power, and the grammar drops "either" before "win." # Draft notes - ch047 ## Paragraph notes

sentences.context: Fire cannot kill a dragon.
sentences.simple: Fire cannot kill a dragon.
sentences.grammar: A proverb-like saying of House Targaryen; Dany uses it to mean that Viserys, killed by heat, was never a true dragon. # Draft notes - ch048 ## Paragraph notes

sentences.context: They follow the man who pays them.
sentences.simple: The City Watch follows whoever pays them.
sentences.grammar: A blunt general truth; "they" are the gold cloaks, and loyalty here is bought, not earned. # Draft notes - ch049 ## Paragraph notes

sentences.context: Our wife is duty. Our mistress is honor.
sentences.simple: Duty is our wife. Honor is our mistress.
sentences.grammar: Two compressed metaphors; a brother's only marriage is to duty and honor.

sentences.context: I did warn you not to trust me, you know.
sentences.simple: I did warn you not to trust me, you know.
sentences.grammar: Past tense for an earlier warning; the mild, polite tone ("you know") makes the betrayal colder. # Draft notes - ch051 ## Paragraph notes

sentences.context: She stuck him with the pointy end, driving the blade upward with a wild, hysterical strength.
sentences.simple: She stabbed him with the sharp end, thrusting the blade upward with wild, terrified strength.
sentences.grammar: "The pointy end" is Jon's childish lesson about swords; the participle phrase "driving the blade upward" describes how she did it. # Draft notes - ch052 ## Paragraph notes

sentences.context: In the songs, the knights never screamed nor begged for mercy.
sentences.simple: In the songs, the knights never screamed or begged for mercy.
sentences.grammar: "Nor" after "never" reinforces the negative; the sentence contrasts Sansa's romantic stories with real battle.

sentences.context: Cold and dead they were, and they hated iron and fire and the touch of the sun, and every living creature with hot blood in its veins.
sentences.simple: Cold and dead they were, and they hated iron and fire and sunlight, and every living thing with warm blood.
sentences.grammar: Inverted word order ("Cold and dead they were") for storytelling emphasis; "the touch of the sun" means sunlight.

sentences.context: but doubtless you only meant to cut my meat.
sentences.simple: But no doubt you only meant to cut my meat.
sentences.grammar: A deadpan joke; Robb pretends the drawn sword was only meant for carving, making the Greatjon's violence look ridiculous.

sentences.context: I will take my khalasar west to where the world ends, and ride the wooden horses across the black salt water as no khal has done before.
sentences.simple: I will lead my khalasar west to the end of the world and sail ships across the sea as no khal has ever done.
sentences.grammar: "Wooden horses" is Drogo's word for ships; "as no khal has done before" is a boast of doing what none have dared. # Draft notes - ch056 ## Paragraph notes

sentences.context: Laughter is poison to fear.
sentences.simple: Laughter destroys fear.
sentences.grammar: A compressed saying; "poison to" means "fatal to" — if men laugh at Robb, they will never fear him.

sentences.context: Frey only takes the field when the scent of victory is in the air, and all he smells now is ruin.
sentences.simple: Frey only joins a war when victory seems certain, and right now all he can smell is defeat.
sentences.grammar: "The scent of victory" and "smells ruin" extend the smell metaphor; the sentence explains Walder Frey's nickname, the Late Lord Frey.

sentences.context: Perhaps Lord Stannis will chance to sit on it when he takes your throne.”
sentences.simple: Perhaps Lord Stannis will happen to sit on it when he takes your throne.
sentences.grammar: A parting insult disguised as politeness; Barristan predicts Joffrey will lose the throne to Stannis.

sentences.context: why is it always the innocents who suffer most, when you high lords play your game of thrones?
sentences.simple: Why is it always the innocent who suffer most when you high lords play your game of thrones?
sentences.grammar: A rhetorical question as moral accusation; "play your game of thrones" treats power politics as a cruel game. # Draft notes - ch060 ## Paragraph notes

sentences.context: I’ll match you son for son, and I’ll still have eighteen when yours are all dead.”
sentences.simple: I will match you son for son, and I will still have eighteen left when all of yours are dead.
sentences.grammar: A boast built on numbers; Walder's huge family is his pride and his weapon. # Draft notes - ch061 ## Paragraph notes

sentences.context: A craven can be as brave as any man, when there is nothing to fear.
sentences.simple: A coward can seem as brave as anyone when there is nothing to be afraid of.
sentences.grammar: A paradox about courage; the real test is choosing when it costs something. # Draft notes - ch062 ## Paragraph notes

sentences.context: Does the horse breed with the sheep?
sentences.simple: Does a horse mate with a sheep?
sentences.grammar: A rhetorical question as mockery; Qotho uses the Dothraki's horse/sheep imagery to say the peoples must not mix.

sentences.context: the army of Lord Tywin Lannister unfolded like an iron rose, thorns gleaming.
sentences.simple: Lord Tywin's army spread out like an iron rose, its thorns gleaming.
sentences.grammar: A simile; "unfolded" compares the deploying army to a blooming flower, but made of iron.

sentences.context: I would offer you my sword, but I seem to have mislaid it.”
sentences.simple: I would surrender my sword to you, but I seem to have lost it.
sentences.grammar: "Mislaid" is a polite word for lost; Jaime's joke keeps his dignity in defeat.

sentences.context: Only death may pay for life.
sentences.simple: Only death can pay for life.
sentences.grammar: The law of bloodmagic; "may" here means "can," stating what is possible, not permission. # Draft notes - ch066 ## Paragraph notes

sentences.context: So long as I am your king, treason shall never go unpunished.
sentences.simple: As long as I am your king, treason will never go unpunished.
sentences.grammar: "So long as" = "as long as"; "shall" gives Joffrey's words a cold, formal finality.

sentences.context: Shut your mouth and close your eyes, boy.
sentences.simple: Shut your mouth and close your eyes, boy.
sentences.grammar: Yoren calls her "boy" to enforce her disguise — and spares her from watching her father's death. # Draft notes - ch067 ## Paragraph notes

sentences.context: we… we shall need to find a stonecarver who knew his likeness well…
sentences.simple: We will need to find a sculptor who knew what he looked like.
sentences.grammar: The broken sentence shows Luwin's shock; "likeness" means his appearance — for his tomb statue. # Draft notes - ch068 ## Paragraph notes

sentences.context: “Life is not a song, sweetling,” he’d told her.
sentences.simple: Life is not a song, sweetling.
sentences.grammar: Littlefinger's lesson: real life does not follow story rules, and happy endings are not promised.

sentences.context: All it would take was a shove, she told herself.
sentences.simple: All it would take was a shove, she told herself.
sentences.grammar: The flat, simple sentence mirrors the simplicity of the thought — murder as one small push. # Draft notes - ch069 ## Paragraph notes

sentences.context: When the sun rises in the west and sets in the east,” said Mirri Maz Duur.
sentences.simple: "When the sun rises in the west and sets in the east," said Mirri Maz Duur.
sentences.grammar: A prophecy of impossibilities — a poetic way of saying "never."

sentences.context: You’ll have an easier time drinking wine from that cup than you will convincing Robb Stark to make peace now.
sentences.simple: You will sooner drink wine from that smashed cup than convince Robb Stark to make peace now.
sentences.grammar: The shattered cup becomes the argument: peace is as impossible as un-breaking it.

sentences.context: You are my son.
sentences.simple: You are my son.
sentences.grammar: Four words, and Tyrion hears what they really mean: Jaime is lost, so you will have to do. # Draft notes - ch071 ## Paragraph notes

sentences.context: When dead men come hunting in the night, do you think it matters who sits the Iron Throne?
sentences.simple: When the dead hunt at night, does it matter who sits the Iron Throne?
sentences.grammar: The rhetorical question reframes everything: the true war is against the dead, not for a crown.

sentences.context: Give me Cersei Lannister, Lord Karstark, and you would see how gentle a woman can be,” Catelyn replied.
sentences.simple: Give me Cersei Lannister, and you would see how gentle a woman can be.
sentences.grammar: The threat is wrapped in courtesy; "gentle" turns ironic and menacing.

sentences.context: It was the dragons we married, and the dragons are all dead!
sentences.simple: We married the dragons, and the dragons are all dead!
sentences.grammar: The Greatjon's history in one line: the North bent the knee to Targaryens, who are gone — so the oath dies with them. # Draft notes - ch073 ## Paragraph notes

sentences.context: She was the blood of the dragon, and the fire was in her.
sentences.simple: She was the blood of the dragon, and the fire was in her.
sentences.grammar: The sentence states her nature as fact; the fire cannot harm its own kin.

sentences.context: I am Daenerys Stormborn, daughter of dragons, bride of dragons, mother of dragons, don’t you see?
sentences.simple: I am Daenerys Stormborn: daughter of dragons, bride of dragons, mother of dragons — don't you see?
sentences.grammar: The triple title builds to her new identity; the repeated question demands the world recognize it. # Draft notes - ch074 (House Baratheon) ## Paragraph notes
